readme.def: A text file (usually `README.md`) at the top of a repository that explains what the project is and how to use it.
levels: A README is like the note taped to a toy box that tells you what's inside and how to play with it before you open it up. Every good project has one sitting right at the top, waiting to be read first.

A README is a plain text file, almost always named `README.md`, that sits in the top folder of a repository and explains what the project does, how to set it up, and how to run it. It's usually the first thing anyone opens when they land on a new repo, before reading any code. Traffic1 has one that should say what the traffic model predicts and how to get it running.

A README is written in Markdown (`README.md`), a simple text format with `#` for headings and backticks for code, which GitHub renders as a formatted page automatically whenever you view the repository. A good README answers, in order, what the project does, how to install it, and how to run it, so a stranger (or you, in six months) doesn't have to read the source code just to get started. Editing it is exactly like editing any other tracked file: change it, `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`.

The README is the repository's front door, and its accuracy tends to decay as code changes underneath it, since nothing enforces that it stays in sync with the scripts it describes. A README that documents exact commands, not just prose describing what they roughly do, is the difference between a project someone can actually run from a fresh clone and one only the original author can. Conventions vary, but a one-paragraph summary, install steps, and a usage example cover most of what a reader needs before diving into code.

At team scale, a stale README is worse than none, since it actively misleads rather than simply being silent, which is why some teams treat README accuracy as something CI checks, running its documented setup commands against a fresh environment and failing the build if they break. A README documents the happy path, and its limits show up exactly in the cases this course cares about, environment quirks, data credentials, timezone handling, that are too specific for a top-level file and belong in dedicated docs it should link to instead of duplicating.

Across a large codebase, README quality is one of the cheapest, highest-leverage signals of a team's engineering discipline, since it costs little to write well and its absence or staleness compounds into hours of onboarding friction multiplied across every new engineer. Internal tooling increasingly templates and lints READMEs the same way code is linted, checking for required sections and even executing the documented quickstart in CI, treating documentation as a build artifact rather than an afterthought.

pull-request.def: A request on GitHub to merge one branch's commits into another, reviewed (even by yourself) before it merges.
levels: A pull request is like showing your parent a drawing before you tape it into the family scrapbook, so someone can look it over first. GitHub keeps a little page just for that one look-over.

A pull request, or PR, is how you ask GitHub to merge the commits on one branch into another, usually into `main`. It shows every changed line side by side so you, or someone else, can read the diff before agreeing to merge it. Even working alone, opening a pull request instead of merging straight to `main` gives you one more chance to catch a mistake.

A pull request compares two branches and shows their diff on a GitHub page, where you or a reviewer can leave comments on specific lines before clicking Merge. You open one after pushing a branch (`git push origin feature-branch`) by visiting the repository on GitHub, which offers to create a PR from the branch it just saw pushed. Required checks, like a test suite, can be configured to block the Merge button until they pass, so a pull request is also where automated tests get their say.

A pull request is not a git concept at all, it's a layer GitHub built on top of git's branches and commits, so the same PR can be closed, reopened, or have new commits pushed onto it without git itself knowing anything about 'pull requests.' Reviewing your own PR before merging, reading the diff as if someone else wrote it, catches a surprising number of mistakes invisible while writing the code, since diff view highlights exactly what changed rather than the surrounding context your memory fills in automatically. A small, focused PR is far easier to review well than a large one mixing several unrelated changes.

At team scale, pull requests are where code review, CI, and branch protection rules intersect: a repository can require a passing test suite, a minimum number of approvals, and no unresolved comment threads before the merge button unlocks, turning 'please review this' into an enforced gate rather than a polite request. The PR description becomes part of the historical record, explaining why a change was made, which is often more valuable months later than the diff itself. Long-lived PRs that sit unreviewed accumulate merge conflicts and reviewer fatigue, which is why small, frequent PRs are the healthier default.

At Apple's scale, the pull request is the unit that CI, static analysis, security scanning, and release engineering all attach to, so a 'pull request' is really a bundle of automated and human judgments that has to converge before code reaches production. Tooling around PRs, required reviewers by code ownership, automatic test selection based on what changed, becomes its own engineering discipline once thousands of engineers merge into the same codebase daily.

makefile.def: A file named `Makefile` listing named targets and the shell commands each one runs; `make target` runs them, skipping work that is already up to date.
levels: A Makefile is a list of chores with their own names, like 'clean-room' or 'walk-dog,' so you can just say the chore's name and the computer does every step for you. Say `make clean-room` and it happens, in order, every time.

A Makefile is a plain text file, named exactly `Makefile`, that lists named jobs called targets, each followed by the shell commands that do that job. Typing `make setup` in the terminal looks up the target named `setup` and runs its commands. It's a way of writing down 'here is how to do this common task' once, so you never have to remember or retype the steps.

A Makefile target looks like `setup:` on its own line, followed by indented shell commands underneath it; running `make setup` executes those commands in order. A target can depend on another target, written `test: setup`, meaning `make test` runs `setup` first, so you never forget a setup step. `make` also skips a target whose output file already exists and is newer than its inputs, which is its real superpower for a pipeline: rerun `make all` and only the stages that actually changed re-run.

Make's dependency model was designed for compiling files, only rebuild a `.o` if its `.c` changed, and applying that same timestamp logic to a data pipeline works cleanly as long as every stage's output is a real file make can check the age of, which is why pipeline Makefiles declare each script's output file as its target rather than an abstract task name. A `.PHONY` target, like `test`, which produces no file, tells make not to apply timestamp logic to it, always running it when asked. Variables and pattern rules let a Makefile avoid repeating itself across many similar targets.

Make's implicit, timestamp-based rebuild logic is also its biggest footgun: touching a file without changing its content, clock skew between machines, or a script that writes its output before finishing successfully can all fool make into thinking work is done when it isn't, which is why serious data pipelines increasingly track content hashes instead of timestamps. Make has no real understanding of a pipeline's data, only of files and their ages, so a Makefile is a thin, textual encoding of a dependency graph that a proper workflow orchestrator represents explicitly, with logging, retries and visualization make itself does not provide.

At scale, `make`-shaped build systems like Bazel and Buck still underlie an enormous amount of infrastructure precisely because the dependency-graph idea is right, even though `make` itself is showing its age; these successors add hermetic, reproducible builds and remote caching plain make's file-timestamp model can't provide. For a data or ML pipeline specifically, the open engineering question is the same one make raised decades ago for compilers: how to know precisely what changed, so only the necessary, and never the unnecessary, work reruns.

stage.def: One numbered step of the project's own pipeline plan (stage 1, stage 2, ...); each stage corresponds to one or more of the numbered scripts.
levels: Think of building a sandwich in steps: first the bread, then the cheese, then the meat. Each step has a number, and this project's own recipe calls each step a 'stage.'

A stage is one numbered step in Traffic1's own plan for turning raw traffic files into a trained model, like 'stage 2: collect 511 incidents' or 'stage 5: engineer features.' The plan documents from phase 0 lay out every stage in order, and the numbered scripts in the repo (`02_collect_events.py`, `10_clean_pems.py`, and so on) are how each stage actually gets done. When a lesson says 'the stage 2 change,' it means a change to the collecting step specifically.

The project's plan breaks the whole pipeline into ordered stages, each reading the previous stage's output and writing its own, and the numbered scripts map onto them (roughly: stage 1 collects PeMS, stage 2 collects 511 events, later stages clean, label, engineer features, and train). Phase pages refer to 'stage 2' or 'stage 5' as shorthand for this numbering, assuming you've read the plan documents in phase 0's resources; if a stage number is unfamiliar, `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md` is where it's spelled out. Stage numbers don't always match script filename prefixes one to one, since one stage can span more than one script.

Naming stages explicitly, rather than letting the numbered scripts imply an order, lets the plan documents describe data contracts between stages, what stage 2 must produce for stage 3 to consume, independent of exactly which script implements which stage. This separation matters because scripts get refactored, split, or merged far more often than the conceptual pipeline stages themselves change, so the stage numbering is the more stable vocabulary to reference in documentation and code review.

A recurring failure mode in numbered pipelines is stage drift: a script gets renumbered or split, but references to 'stage 5' scattered across docs, commit messages and code comments don't get updated, so the label silently stops matching reality. Treating the plan document as the single source of truth for what each stage means, and linking to it rather than re-describing stages ad hoc, is the cheap fix most projects skip until it costs them a confused afternoon.

At production scale, informal stage numbering like this gives way to an explicit DAG tracked by a workflow orchestrator, where each stage is a node with declared inputs, outputs and a version, so 'stage 5' is no longer a shared convention people have to remember correctly but a queryable object the system enforces and can render as a diagram.

supervised-learning.def: Training a model on examples that already have the right answer attached; classification is supervised learning where the answer is one of a fixed set of categories.
levels: Supervised learning is like practicing spelling words with an answer key right next to you: you guess, then check, then get a little better each time. Classification is when the answer is always one of a few choices, like 'slow' or 'not slow,' instead of any number at all.

In supervised learning, you show the computer lots of examples that already have the correct answer attached, like a station's past readings paired with whether it turned out to be slow 30 minutes later, and it learns a pattern connecting the two. Classification is the kind of supervised learning where the answer is one of a small set of categories, here just two: slow or not slow. This is different from asking the computer to predict an exact number, which is a related but different job called regression.

Supervised learning fits a function from inputs (features) to a known target using a training set where every row's target is already known, then checks how well that function predicts the target on rows it did not train on. Binary classification is supervised learning where the target takes exactly one of two values, here 1 (inside a slow episode) or 0 (not), and the model's job is to output a probability that the answer is 1. This differs from unsupervised learning, which looks for structure in data with no target column at all, something this course does not use for the traffic model itself.

Formally, supervised learning fits f(x) ≈ y from a training set of (x, y) pairs by minimizing a loss that measures how wrong f's predictions are, and feature engineering, model choice and evaluation in this course all exist to make that fit generalize to rows the model has never seen. Binary classification is the special case where y is 0 or 1; multiclass classification generalizes to more categories, and regression predicts a continuous number instead. What makes classification distinct in practice is that its natural output is a probability, not a hard label, and metrics like average precision are built specifically around ranking and thresholding that probability rather than minimizing squared error the way regression does.

The supervised/unsupervised split is cleaner in textbooks than in practice: this project's 'typical speed' profile, used to define the slow-episode label itself, is effectively an unsupervised summary statistic feeding into a supervised label, and self-supervised methods blur the line further. A subtlety specific to classification is that a model's discriminative power (can it rank positives above negatives) and its calibration (are its probabilities honest) are separate properties a single accuracy or average-precision number does not jointly capture, which is why this course tracks both.

In production, 'classification' rarely stays this clean: label noise, class definitions that drift as stakeholders' needs change, and multi-label or hierarchical variants are the norm, and most of an applied ML engineer's time goes into managing that mess rather than choosing between logistic regression and a neural network. The open question that recurs across every classification deployment is less 'which model' and more 'is the label itself still measuring what we actually care about,' since a perfectly fit model against a stale or wrong label definition is a confidently wrong system.

loop-detector.def: A wire coil buried in the pavement that senses a vehicle passing over it by the change it causes in a magnetic field; most PeMS stations use a pair of these.
levels: Under some roads there's a wire coiled up like a spring buried in the pavement. When a car's metal rolls over it, it makes a tiny change the wire can feel, like stepping on a hidden doormat.

A loop detector is a loop of wire buried just under the road's surface that senses when a car, which is mostly metal, passes over it. PeMS stations often use two loops spaced a known distance apart: timing how long a car takes to cross from one loop to the other gives its speed directly. This 'loop' is a physical wire coil in the road, not the same word as a Python `for` loop.

A loop detector works by induction: current in the buried wire coil creates a magnetic field, and a vehicle's metal body passing over briefly changes that field in a way the sensor's electronics can detect and time. A 'single-loop' station has only one coil and has to estimate speed indirectly from flow and occupancy using an assumed vehicle length (the g-factor), while a 'double-loop' station times a vehicle crossing two coils directly for a more accurate reading. Loop detectors are the dominant sensing technology behind PeMS's mainline stations, but they fail in ordinary ways: a cracked loop, a miscalibrated g-factor, or a lane-assignment error, all of which show up as suspicious readings rather than a clean error message.

The physical measurement a loop detector actually makes is occupancy, the fraction of time a vehicle is present over the loop, and everything else, flow, speed, is derived from that raw signal combined with timing and, for single-loop stations, an assumed vehicle length; speed from a single loop is fundamentally an estimate, not a direct measurement, and its error grows exactly when that assumption breaks down, like during a spike in truck traffic. Loop detectors are also spatially fixed and relatively expensive to install and maintain compared to newer technologies (radar, cameras, connected-vehicle probes), part of why PeMS coverage is uneven.

Because loop detectors report occupancy and count directly but infer speed, their failure modes are asymmetric: a chattering or stuck loop typically corrupts occupancy and flow first, and speed often looks locally sane even from a partly broken detector because it's computed from a smoothing model rather than reported raw, exactly the kind of error a naive speed-only sanity check misses. Detector health has to be assessed from all three measured quantities and their mutual consistency, not from any one column looking reasonable in isolation.

At the scale of a whole metro network, loop detectors are being supplemented and in places replaced by radar, video analytics and connected-vehicle or phone-probe data, each with a different, non-overlapping failure mode, and a mature traffic-sensing system fuses all of them with an explicit per-source reliability model rather than trusting any one technology as ground truth. Transferring a model trained on fixed-loop data to a probe-data-dominated region with completely different coverage and error characteristics is one of the more consequential open problems in traffic forecasting at scale.

time-series.def: A sequence of values for the same thing, in time order, one entry per time step, like one station's speed reading every five minutes for a month.
levels: A time series is a list of the same measurement taken again and again, like writing down the temperature outside every single morning for a month. Read top to bottom, it tells a little story of how things changed.

A time series is a table or list of values for one thing, in order by time, with one value, or row, per time step. One station's readings for a month, sorted by timestamp, is exactly a time series: 288 rows a day, each five minutes after the last. Unlike a random pile of rows, a time series has an order that matters: row 100 comes right before row 101, and shuffling the rows would destroy real information.

A time series is data indexed by time, and its defining property is that nearby points are usually correlated: traffic speed five minutes from now is much more like traffic speed right now than like traffic speed a random day away. `s.sort_values("timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)` is exactly how this course turns a jumble of one station's rows into a proper time series, ordered so row position means time position. Lag and rolling features (`shift(k)`, `rolling(n)`) only make sense on a time series, since they depend entirely on knowing which row came before which.

Formally, a time series is a sequence of observations x_t indexed by time t, and its central modeling challenge is that observations are not independent and identically distributed the way a typical machine-learning dataset's rows are assumed to be, so techniques like random train/validation splits leak information or mis-estimate performance when applied naively without respecting time order. This course's panel of many stations, each its own time series, is a specific and common structure called panel data, and splitting it correctly, by time, and often by station too, is one of the most consequential correctness decisions in the whole pipeline.

Time series have properties with no analogue in i.i.d. data: autocorrelation, seasonality, and non-stationarity, each of which this course's own labeling and evaluation choices, a per-station-and-slot profile, rolling-origin evaluation, exist specifically to handle. A common and expensive mistake is computing a summary statistic across an entire time series and using it as a feature at every timestamp, which silently leaks future information into earlier rows unless the statistic is computed using only data available up to that point.

At production scale, time series problems span from a single sensor's five-minute readings to millions of concurrent series, and the systems challenge shifts from 'model one series well' to 'model many related series efficiently while sharing statistical strength between them without one noisy series corrupting a model shared across all of them.' Foundation-model-style approaches that pretrain on many time series at once, transferring to a new series with little or no fine-tuning, are an active research frontier traffic forecasting is a natural, if under-explored, application area for.

regular-expression.def: A pattern written in a small symbolic language for matching and pulling text out of a string, like finding "I-880" inside "Collision on I-880 N".
levels: A regular expression is like a shape-sorter toy for words: you describe the shape of text you're looking for, like 'starts with I, then a dash, then some numbers,' and it finds every piece of text shaped like that.

A regular expression, or regex, is a short pattern written in its own tiny language that describes a shape of text to search for, instead of one exact word. `\d` means 'any digit,' `+` means 'one or more of the thing before it,' so `\d+` matches a run of digits like '880.' Python's `re` module uses these patterns to find or pull pieces out of text, like pulling the freeway number out of a road name.

In a regex, a plain letter matches itself, `\d` matches any digit, `\s` matches any whitespace, `+` means one or more, `*` means zero or more, `?` means zero or one (optional), `|` means or, and parentheses `(...)` mark a group you can pull out separately. `re.search(r'(I-\d+|SR-\d+)\s*([NSEW])?', 'Collision on I-880 N')` looks for either 'I-' or 'SR-' followed by digits, then an optional direction letter; `m.group(1)` and `m.group(2)` retrieve the two parenthesized pieces it found. This course uses regex to pull a route and direction out of 511's free-text road names.

A regex engine compiles the pattern and then scans the input string for the leftmost match; `re.compile()` pre-compiles a pattern once for reuse rather than re-parsing it on every call, which matters when matching against many rows. Greedy quantifiers (`+`, `*`) consume as much as they can before backtracking to satisfy the rest of the pattern, while lazy counterparts (`+?`, `*?`) consume as little as possible, a distinction that changes what a pattern matches on ambiguous input. Character classes (`[NSEW]`), anchors (`^`, `$`), and named groups are the other pieces that turn 'find roughly this' into a precise, testable pattern.

Regexes are a genuinely separate, small formal language, and their real danger at scale is catastrophic backtracking: certain patterns combined with certain inputs cause exponential-time matching, a denial-of-service risk if a regex ever runs against untrusted input. Regexes are also notoriously write-only: a pattern obvious while writing it is often unreadable a month later, which is why serious codebases pair a nontrivial regex with a comment showing example matches and a test asserting exactly what it does and does not match.

At production scale, hand-written regexes for parsing loosely structured text, like 511's free-text road names, are a known source of silent data-quality bugs, since a pattern tuned against a sample of today's data quietly stops matching, or starts mismatching, the moment the upstream format shifts even slightly, with nothing necessarily raising an error. Production text-parsing pipelines increasingly pair regex extraction with monitoring, a dashboard tracking what fraction of rows a pattern successfully matches over time, precisely because a regex has no concept of 'I don't recognize this,' it either matches or silently doesn't.

http.def: HTTP is the request-and-response language a program uses to talk to a web server; a URL is the address of what you're asking for, like `https://511.org/traffic`.
levels: A URL is an address, like a house address but for a page on the internet. HTTP is the polite way computers knock on that address's door and ask for what's inside, then wait for an answer to come back.

A URL is the address of something on the web, like `https://api.511.org/traffic/events`. HTTP is the set of rules a program follows to ask a server at that address for something and get an answer back, called a request and a response. When Python's `requests.get(url)` runs, it's sending an HTTP request to that URL and waiting for the server's response, usually text or JSON.

An HTTP request has a method (`GET` to fetch data, `POST` to send data), a URL, and optional parameters; `requests.get(url, params={'api_key': KEY})` sends a GET request to `url` with `api_key` attached as a query parameter, visible right in the URL after a `?`. The response carries a status code, 200 means success, 404 means 'not found,' 401 or 403 usually means a missing or bad API key, and a body, which `.json()` parses into a Python dictionary when the server sent JSON. A request can simply fail (no internet, the server is down), which is why the collector script wraps every request in `try/except`.

HTTP is a stateless, text-based protocol: each request-response pair is independent, carrying its own headers and body, with no memory of previous requests unless the application layers something like a token on top. `requests` handles the low-level connection details so application code only deals with a URL, parameters, and the response object; `resp.raise_for_status()` turns an HTTP error status into a Python exception instead of silently returning bad data. Rate limits, timeouts, and retries are the practical concerns that separate 'code that fetches one URL once' from 'code that reliably polls a real API,' which is most of what a robust collector script actually is.

HTTP's statelessness pushes state management, sessions, retries, idempotency, entirely onto the client, which is why a naive poller that assumes 'ask again' is always safe can double-count an event if a response is lost after the server processed it but before the client received it. Distinguishing which HTTP failures are safe to retry (a timeout, a 500, likely transient) from which are not (a 400, meaning the request itself was malformed) is a real design decision every polling script this course builds has to make, explicitly or by accident.

At production scale, 'just call requests.get' gives way to managed HTTP clients with connection pooling, circuit breakers, and distributed tracing that stitches one logical operation across many services' HTTP calls together, because a single unhandled slow endpoint can otherwise cascade into an outage for everything depending on it. Any system built on an external HTTP API, like this course's dependence on 511 and PeMS, inherits that API's uptime, rate limits and undocumented behavior changes as a permanent operational risk.

bounding-box.def: A rectangle described by its min and max latitude and longitude, used to test whether a point (like an incident) falls inside an area (like Fremont).
levels: A bounding box is like drawing a rectangle around your neighborhood on a map and asking 'is this thing inside my rectangle or outside it?'

A bounding box is a rectangle on a map, described by its westmost, eastmost, northmost and southmost edges, using latitude and longitude. To check whether an incident happened near Fremont, the collector script compares the incident's own latitude and longitude against Fremont's bounding box: if both fall between the box's edges, the incident counts as touching Fremont.

A bounding box is stored as four numbers: min longitude, min latitude, max longitude, max latitude, defining a rectangle's edges. Checking whether a point is inside it is four comparisons: `min_lon <= lon <= max_lon and min_lat <= lat <= max_lat`; if all four hold, the point is inside. `event_touches_fremont()` in `02_collect_events.py` does exactly this check against a bounding box drawn around Fremont's freeways, which is why an incident with no location, or one just outside the box, gets filtered out even if it's nearby in spirit.

A bounding box is a coarse spatial filter, and its rectangular shape means it doesn't track a real region's actual boundary; a box drawn tightly enough to contain Fremont's freeways will also include some genuinely unrelated area, and one drawn to exclude that area risks clipping a real Fremont incident near an edge. This tradeoff, false positives near the box's corners versus false negatives at its true boundary, is inherent to any rectangle-based spatial filter and is why a bounding box is a cheap first pass, not a precise geographic test.

A subtlety with any lat/lon bounding box is that longitude degrees are not a constant physical distance, they shrink toward the poles as cos(latitude), so a box that looks square in coordinates is not square in miles; at Fremont's latitude this distortion is small but not zero, and grows quickly for code reused at higher latitudes without adjustment. A more accurate spatial filter, a polygon following the actual freeway corridor, trades this simplicity for real implementation cost, which is why this course starts with a bounding box and treats a tighter geometry as a later refinement.

At production scale, bounding-box filtering is the first, cheapest stage of a spatial pipeline, it can use a simple index and reject most points in constant time, typically followed by a more precise geometric test, point-in-polygon or distance-to-road-network, only on the much smaller set of points the bounding box didn't already reject. Real geographic systems also have to handle the antimeridian and coordinate reference system mismatches, edge cases a fixed local region like Fremont never has to face, but code reused globally eventually will.

wildcard.def: A pattern like `*.csv` that the shell expands into every matching filename before running the command, so `*` stands for "anything."
levels: A wildcard is like saying 'any toy that starts with car' instead of naming every single toy car one by one. The star `*` means 'fill in the blank with anything.'

A wildcard is a special character the shell understands, mainly `*`, meaning 'any text at all.' Typing `ls *.csv` doesn't run a program called `*.csv`; the shell first looks in the current folder, finds every filename ending in `.csv`, and hands `ls` that whole list instead. This is called globbing, and it works the same way for any command, not just `ls`.

Before running a command, the shell expands a glob pattern like `*.txt.gz` into every matching filename in the current folder, sorted alphabetically, and passes that expanded list as separate arguments to the command; `for f in *.txt.gz; do echo $f; done` runs the loop body once per matching file. `?` matches exactly one character where `*` matches any number, and `[abc]` matches any one of the listed characters. If no file matches, most shells leave the pattern unexpanded, a classic source of a script silently trying to open a file literally named `*.txt.gz`.

Glob expansion happens entirely in the shell, before the named program ever runs, which is why quoting a glob pattern (`'*.csv'`) suppresses expansion when you want the literal characters, for example to pass a pattern into `find -name`, which does its own matching internally instead. Glob patterns are deliberately simpler than regular expressions, they only handle filename-shaped matching (`*`, `?`, character classes), not the general text patterns a regex can express, which is a feature, not a limitation, for the narrow job of naming files.

A well-known glob footgun is a folder with many thousands of matching files exceeding a shell's maximum argument-list length, which makes `*` expansion fail with an 'argument list too long' error unrelated to the command's own logic; `find ... -exec` or `xargs` sidestep this by feeding filenames in batches instead of expanding them all into one command line. Another is an unquoted glob matching zero files silently passing the literal pattern string through, a quiet, easy-to-miss bug in a script built to run unattended.

At scale, shell globbing over a live filesystem doesn't scale to buckets holding millions of objects, since globbing implies listing the whole directory first, so production data pipelines replace it with prefix-based or partition-aware listing APIs that avoid ever enumerating more than what's actually needed. The underlying idea, a compact pattern standing in for a set of names, survives in those systems too, just implemented very differently under the hood for scale.

with-statement.def: `with expr as name:` runs setup before the indented block and guaranteed cleanup after it, even if the block raises an error; `with open(path) as f:` is the common example.
levels: A `with` block is like borrowing a library book: the `with` makes sure that no matter what happens while you're reading it, the book gets returned to the shelf when you're done, automatically.

`with open('file.csv') as f:` opens a file, gives it the name `f` for the indented lines underneath, and automatically closes the file again once those lines finish, even if something goes wrong partway through. Without `with`, you'd have to remember to call `f.close()` yourself, and a crash before that line would leave the file open. It's the standard, safe way to work with files in Python.

The general shape is `with expression as name:`, where `expression` is something Python knows how to enter (do setup) and exit (do cleanup); a file object does this by opening on enter and closing on exit. The cleanup always runs, even if the indented block raises an exception, which is exactly the guarantee `try/finally` gives by hand, just shorter to write. `with open(path) as f:` followed by indented lines that read or write `f` is the pattern used throughout this course's file-handling code.

Under the hood, `with` calls the expression's `__enter__` method before the block and its `__exit__` method after, whether the block finished normally or raised, which is what makes `with` the right tool for anything holding a resource that must be released: files, network connections, locks, database cursors. Multiple resources can be managed in one `with` statement, and writing your own context manager, either as a class with `__enter__`/`__exit__` or with `@contextlib.contextmanager`, is how a codebase extends this guarantee to its own resources.

A common mistake is assuming `with` protects against every kind of failure; it guarantees `__exit__` runs, but if `__exit__` itself does something fallible that can still raise, and a badly written context manager can swallow an exception silently by returning a truthy value from `__exit__`, a subtle bug since the calling code has no obvious sign anything went wrong. In data pipelines, `with` around a file write is not by itself atomic: a crash mid-write still leaves a partial file on disk unless the code writes to a temporary path and renames it on success, a pattern `with` makes easy to add but does not provide automatically.

At scale, context managers generalize into resource-management patterns across async code (`async with`), distributed locks, and transaction boundaries in databases, where the same enter/exit guarantee has to hold even when execution is interrupted by a process crash or a preempted container, considerably harder to guarantee than a single process's file handle. The core idea stays exactly the same as the one-line file example: acquire, do work, release, no matter what.

ln.def: The power you'd raise a fixed base to, to get a number; ln is log base e, and it turns multiplying into adding.
levels: A logarithm is a "how many times" question: how many times do you have to double a thing to reach 8? Three times, since 2×2×2=8, so the logarithm of 8 (base 2) is 3. It's a way of asking "how big is this, really" using multiplying instead of counting up by ones.

A logarithm answers the question "what power do I raise this base to, to get this number?" log₁₀(100) = 2 because 10² = 100. In this course, the natural logarithm, written ln, uses Euler's number e (about 2.718) as its base instead of 10, and it shows up constantly in machine learning because it turns a model's confidence, a number between 0 and 1, into a penalty that grows huge as that confidence gets closer to being completely wrong.

log_b(x) is the power you raise b to, to get x; ln(x) means log base e. Two facts matter here: ln(1) = 0 (no power needed to get 1), and ln(x) → −∞ as x → 0 (getting a probability close to 0 wrong costs an enormous penalty). ln turns multiplication into addition, ln(ab) = ln(a) + ln(b), which is why maximizing a product of many probabilities (the likelihood) is done instead by adding up their logs (the log-likelihood). In `03_train_from_scratch.py`, `np.log(p)` computes ln(p), and cross-entropy is built entirely from two calls to it.

The natural log is preferred throughout statistics and ML because its derivative is the simplest of any log base, d/dx ln(x) = 1/x, which is exactly what makes the cross-entropy gradient collapse to p − y once the chain rule cancels it against the sigmoid's own derivative. Log-probabilities are also what numerical code actually works with once probabilities get extreme: multiplying a thousand small probabilities together underflows to exactly 0 in floating point, while summing their logs stays a well-behaved, precise number. `np.clip` before `np.log` in this course's loss function exists precisely to keep ln's input away from 0, where it diverges to −∞.

Because ln(p) is unbounded below as p → 0, any loss built from it is numerically fragile near the extremes, which is why production implementations never call `log` and `sigmoid` as two separate operations on raw scores; they fuse them (the log-sum-exp trick) to cancel the exponential and the logarithm algebraically before either one can overflow or underflow. The log-likelihood's concavity, a direct consequence of log being a concave function, is what makes maximum-likelihood estimation for exponential-family models like the Bernoulli tractable by gradient methods in the first place. A practitioner mistake is forgetting that log and exp are inverses only for compatible bases and positive inputs, so a stray negative number reaching a log call is a silent NaN waiting to propagate, not an error you'll see immediately.

At scale, log-space arithmetic is the default representation for anything resembling a probability once a pipeline chains enough multiplications; speech and language models score entire sequences in log-probability and only exponentiate at the very end, for exactly the underflow reasons above. Mixed-precision training makes this sharper still: float16's dynamic range makes naive probability-space computation unusable for long chains, so log-space or logit-space representations are load-bearing engineering choices, not stylistic ones. Open tooling work continues on making fused numerically-stable kernels (log-softmax, log-sum-exp) the automatic default rather than something an engineer has to remember to reach for.

sigma.def: Two unrelated uses of the same Greek letter: capital Σ means "add up a list"; lowercase σ usually means standard deviation, but inside σ(z) it means the sigmoid function instead.
levels: Σ is a math shorthand for "add all of these up," like a teacher saying "total the whole row" instead of writing out a long plus sign every time. Its lowercase cousin σ shows up in two different jobs depending on where you see it, which can be confusing, so always check what it's sitting next to.

The capital Greek letter Σ (sigma) means "sum everything that follows." Σ pᵢ means "add up every pᵢ in the list," the same thing as writing p₁ + p₂ + p₃ + … by hand, just shorter. The lowercase σ is a completely different piece of notation with two unrelated jobs in this course: on its own, σ usually means standard deviation, how spread out a set of numbers is; written as σ(z) with something in parentheses, it means the sigmoid function instead, the S-curve that turns a score into a probability. They share a letter by historical accident, not because they're related.

Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ xᵢ means "add up xᵢ for every i from 1 to n," so Σᵢ xᵢ² is shorthand for x₁² + x₂² + … + xₙ²; you'll see it in formulas like variance, σ² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ)², and entropy, H = −Σ pᵢ log(pᵢ). Lowercase σ without an argument (as in "σ = 8 mph") means standard deviation; σ with a variable in parentheses, σ(z), is a function call, the sigmoid squashing z into a probability, unrelated to spread. `np.sum(x)` is Σ in code; `x.std()` is σ as standard deviation; `sigmoid(z)` is σ as a function, and this course's code never writes the sigmoid as a bare `sigma`, precisely to keep the two apart.

Overloading σ this way is standard across statistics and ML literature, not a quirk of this course, so reading papers requires tracking which σ a given equation means from context, usually whether it's applied to a number (spread) or to an expression like a weighted sum (a function). Σ generalizes cleanly to double and triple sums, ΣᵢΣⱼ, for matrix and tensor expressions, and to Einstein summation notation, which drops the Σ entirely and treats a repeated index as an implicit sum, the convention `einsum` in numpy and PyTorch is named after. Confusing Σ-as-sum with the summation already implicit in matrix multiplication, X @ w already performs a Σ per row, is a common source of writing a redundant explicit loop over something numpy already vectorizes.

In measure-theoretic probability, Σ as summation is the discrete special case of the general integral ∫, and moving between the two is exactly how discrete formulas (entropy, expectation as Σ x P(x)) generalize to continuous distributions (differential entropy, expectation as ∫ x p(x) dx). The σ-as-sigmoid convention specifically traces to statistics' logistic-function literature and persists in ML despite the standard-deviation clash because sigmoid predates most of deep learning's own notation and nobody has successfully displaced it. A subtler collision: σ also denotes a permutation in some optimization and combinatorics literature, and singular values are sometimes written σᵢ, a third meaning worth recognizing when a paper's context doesn't immediately disambiguate.

At production scale, none of this ambiguity survives into code, where `std()`, `sigmoid()`, and `sum()` are separate, unambiguous function names, which is precisely why translating a paper's dense Σ/σ notation into a correct, readably-named implementation is real, nontrivial work, and a frequent source of subtle bugs when done under time pressure. Documentation and internal wikis that translate literature notation into named variables at the point of first use are an underrated piece of engineering hygiene for exactly this reason. The broader lesson generalizes: any single-letter mathematical notation is locally clear and globally overloaded, so production code favors verbose, unambiguous names over a paper's terse symbols every time the two need to coexist.

partial-derivative.def: ∂f/∂x is the derivative of f with respect to x alone, treating every other input as if it were frozen; the gradient collects one per input.
levels: Imagine a hill whose height depends on how far north you walk AND how far east you walk. A partial derivative asks just one of those questions at a time: "if I only walk east and stop moving north, how steep does it get?" The little curly ∂ is a hint that something else is being held still while you ask.

When a function has more than one input, like a score that depends on several features at once, you can ask how much it changes because of just ONE input, while pretending the others don't move. That's a partial derivative, written with a curly ∂ instead of a straight d, specifically to remind you that other inputs exist but are being held fixed for this one calculation. Do that once for every input, and you have the gradient, the full list of "how much does each one matter."

∂f/∂x means: take the derivative of f with respect to x, treating every other variable as a constant. For the logistic regression loss, ∂loss/∂w means "how much does the loss change if w changes a tiny bit, holding b fixed," and ∂loss/∂b asks the same question about b instead. The curly ∂ (as opposed to the straight d used for a function of one variable) is purely a notational signal that there's more than one input in play; the mechanics of taking the derivative don't change. Stacking every ∂loss/∂(one parameter) into a single list gives the gradient, ∇loss.

Formally, ∂f/∂xᵢ is the ordinary single-variable derivative of the function g(t) = f(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, t, xᵢ₊₁, …, xₙ) evaluated at t = xᵢ, which is exactly "hold everything else fixed" made precise. The full derivative of a multivariable function is the Jacobian, a matrix of every output's partial derivative with respect to every input, and for a single scalar output (a loss), the Jacobian collapses to a row vector that, transposed, is the gradient. The multivariable chain rule composes these as matrix products of Jacobians rather than scalar multiplication, which is the precise statement of what backpropagation computes layer by layer.

Partial derivatives assume the function is differentiable along each axis at the point in question, which can fail even when the full function looks smooth, a subtlety that matters at kinks like ReLU's corner, handled by convention rather than by a literal partial derivative there. Mixed partials, ∂²f/∂x∂y, appear in the Hessian's off-diagonal entries and, by Clairaut's theorem, equal ∂²f/∂y∂x for well-behaved functions, which is why the Hessian is symmetric. Automatic differentiation computes every partial derivative needed for a gradient in roughly the cost of one forward pass, not one pass per parameter, which is the entire reason reverse-mode autodiff, not literally evaluating each ∂f/∂xᵢ from its limit definition, is how every deep learning framework actually works.

At the scale of models with billions of parameters, no partial derivative is ever computed from its textbook limit definition; frameworks build a computation graph and propagate partials backward through recorded operations, and the entire discipline of differentiable programming is about designing systems where every operation, however exotic, has a well-defined local partial derivative to propagate through. Numerical precision of partial derivatives compounds across very deep or very long graphs, which is why mixed-precision training tracks some quantities in higher precision specifically to keep accumulated partials from degrading. An open research question is differentiating through operations that don't have a natural partial derivative at all, discrete choices, simulator steps, sampling, where gradient estimators substitute for a partial derivative that formally doesn't exist.

convex.def: A function shaped like a single bowl, with no separate dips; every local minimum is also the global minimum, so gradient descent can't get stuck.
levels: Imagine a bowl versus a muffin tin. Roll a marble into a bowl from anywhere and it always ends up at the same lowest point. Roll it into a muffin tin and it might get stuck in whichever cup it started closest to. A convex function is the bowl.

A function is convex if its graph is shaped like a single bowl, curving upward everywhere with no separate dips or bumps. That matters for training a model because gradient descent works by rolling downhill, and in a bowl-shaped loss there's only one bottom, so no matter where you start, rolling downhill always gets you to the actual best answer. A function with several separate dips (not convex) can trap gradient descent in a dip that isn't the lowest one.

A function f is convex if the straight line between any two points on its graph never dips below the graph itself, equivalently, if its curvature (its second derivative, or Hessian in several dimensions) never turns negative. Logistic regression's cross-entropy loss is convex in its weights, which is why "every local minimum is global" holds: any point where the gradient is zero is guaranteed to be the actual best fit, not just a locally good one. This is a big part of why logistic regression is a reliable baseline: training can't get stuck the way it sometimes can for a neural network's non-convex loss.

Formally, f is convex if f(λx + (1−λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1−λ)f(y) for every x, y and every λ in [0,1], and it's strictly convex if that inequality is strict, which guarantees a unique minimum rather than merely a connected set of equally good ones. A twice-differentiable function is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere, which for logistic regression's negative log-likelihood is provably true (the Hessian is Xᵀdiag(p(1−p))X), giving convexity a clean, checkable algebraic proof rather than an appeal to intuition. Convexity is what makes a huge body of optimization theory apply cleanly, convergence guarantees, duality, efficient algorithms, and it's precisely what a neural network's stack of nonlinear layers gives up.

Convexity is preserved under many useful operations (a sum of convex functions is convex, the max of convex functions is convex), which is how more complex convex losses, like hinge loss or L1-regularized objectives, get built up and proven convex piece by piece rather than checked from the definition each time. Strict convexity is a stronger, separate property: logistic regression's loss can be convex but not strictly so under perfect separation or collinear features, exactly when coefficients diverge to infinity rather than settling at a unique optimum, a failure that regularization fixes by restoring strict convexity. Non-convex optimization, essentially all of deep learning, forfeits these guarantees entirely, and the modern understanding is that high-dimensional non-convex loss landscapes are dominated by saddle points rather than bad local minima, a different, subtler problem than the one convexity solves.

At production scale, convex models like logistic regression persist specifically because their convexity gives reproducible, debuggable training, two runs converge to the same optimum regardless of initialization, a property large neural networks genuinely lack and that matters when a model's exact behavior needs to be audited or reproduced later. Recent theory shows that gradient descent on logistic loss over separable data still has striking, if subtler, structure (it converges in direction to the max-margin classifier), extending convex-optimization-style guarantees into a regime classical convex analysis wasn't built to describe. An open research thread asks how much of convex optimization's clean theory can be recovered, even approximately, for the non-convex objectives that dominate modern practice.

broadcasting.def: numpy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by automatically stretching the smaller one, so `X @ w + b` can add one bias number to every row of X without a loop.
levels: Imagine handing out one extra cookie to every single kid in a room, even though you only have one cookie in your hand to show. Broadcasting is numpy doing the same trick with numbers: it takes one small piece of information and automatically repeats it across every row or column that needs it.

Broadcasting is numpy's rule for combining two arrays that aren't the same shape, by automatically stretching the smaller one to match, without you writing a loop. If `X` is a table of 1,000 rows and `b` is a single number, `X + b` adds `b` to every single row automatically. That's what happens in logistic regression's score `X @ w + b`: `w` is a list of weights, `b` is one number, and numpy repeats `b` across every row of the result without anyone writing "for each row."

numpy compares two arrays' shapes from the right; dimensions match if they're equal, or if one of them is 1 (in which case that size-1 dimension is stretched to match). A `(1000, 5)` array plus a `(5,)` array broadcasts the second across all 1,000 rows; a `(1000, 5)` array plus a plain number broadcasts the number everywhere. In `sigmoid(X @ w + b)`, `X @ w` has shape `(1000,)` and `b` is a single float, so broadcasting adds it to every row's score in one line, with no explicit loop and no extra memory allocated for a repeated copy of `b`.

Broadcasting's shape-matching rule (align from the right, stretch any size-1 dimension) is convenient exactly because it lets code stay concise and vectorized, but it is also numpy's most common source of silent bugs: a `(100,)` array broadcasting against a `(100, 1)` array combines elementwise into a `(100, 100)` array instead of raising a shape error, because both shapes technically satisfy the rule. This is why printing `.shape` after any operation whose result looks surprising is standard debugging practice, and why explicit reshaping (`x[:, None]` to force a column vector) is preferred over relying on broadcasting to "just work" in code meant to be read later. Broadcasting never allocates a real, stretched copy in memory; the smaller array's values are reused in place, which is part of why it's fast, not just concise.

Broadcasting generalizes past two arrays to any chain of elementwise operations, and getting the semantics wrong compounds silently across a pipeline, a bias vector accidentally broadcast along the wrong axis (stations instead of time steps, say) produces a numerically valid but semantically scrambled result that trains without error and only shows up as unexplained poor accuracy. PyTorch and other frameworks implement the identical broadcasting rule for tensors specifically so numpy intuition transfers, but tensor broadcasting interacts with autograd: a broadcast operation's backward pass must sum gradients back down to the original smaller shape, which is easy to get wrong when writing a custom operation by hand. Explicit `assert` statements on shape at module boundaries are the standard defense against broadcasting mistakes that would otherwise degrade a model's accuracy without ever raising an exception.

At production scale, broadcasting-style implicit shape rules extend into distributed tensor computation, where a broadcast across GPUs or machines has real communication cost that a broadcast within one machine's memory does not, so what reads as one free-form line of numpy can hide a meaningfully expensive collective operation once the same code runs distributed. Compilers for ML workloads (XLA, MLIR) specialize and fuse broadcast operations into hardware kernels precisely because naive broadcasting, implemented literally, would materialize wasteful intermediate copies at scale. An open practical concern in large codebases is that broadcasting's convenience actively discourages the explicit shape annotations that would catch these bugs at review time, which is why some production ML codebases now enforce shape-checked tensor types specifically to trade away some of broadcasting's terseness for caught-at-review-time correctness.

scientific-notation.def: `1e-6` means 1 × 10⁻⁶, or 0.000001; the `e` here means "times ten to the power of," not Euler's number.
levels: `1e-6` is a fast way of writing a really, really tiny number, like one one-millionth, without typing five zeroes. It's just a shortcut, the same tiny number either way.

`1e-6` is Python's way of writing "1 times 10 to the power of −6," which works out to 0.000001, a very small number. The letter `e` here stands for "exponent," not for Euler's number 2.718, which is a completely different, unrelated use of the same letter; you can only tell them apart from where they appear. `1e6` (no minus sign) means 1 times 10 to the power of 6, or one million, a very large number instead.

`NeM` in code means N × 10^M; `1e-6` is 1 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.000001, and `1e6` is 1 × 10⁶ = 1,000,000. This course uses tiny values like `1e-6`, `1e-7` and `eps = 1e-4` to avoid dividing or taking a logarithm of exactly zero, `np.clip(p, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)` keeps p a hair away from 0 and 1 so `np.log(p)` never hits −∞. It also uses large values like `C=1e6` to make a penalty term effectively zero without literally removing it from the formula. Reading `1e-6` as "Euler's number raised to −6" is a real, easy mistake; scientific notation's `e` and Euler's constant `e` are unrelated despite the shared letter.

Scientific notation in code is just a compact literal for a float, `1e-6` and `0.000001` produce the identical IEEE-754 floating-point value, chosen for readability rather than any computational difference; the compact form is preferred specifically because a long run of zeroes is easy to miscount by one digit when hand-typing a threshold like an epsilon or a regularization constant. These magic-looking small constants (`1e-6`, `1e-7`) are almost always there to guard against a specific numerical failure, division by zero, log of zero, not arbitrary tuning knobs, and changing one without understanding which failure it guards against is a common source of code that "still works" but silently stops protecting against the edge case it was written for. Floating-point precision limits how small a meaningful `1e-N` can be: float32 has roughly 7 decimal digits of precision, so an epsilon smaller than about `1e-7` can vanish entirely when added to a number near 1.

The choice of epsilon in `np.clip(p, eps, 1-eps)` trades two failure modes against each other: too large and it visibly biases the loss near confident, correct predictions; too small and it fails to prevent the very overflow it exists for once floating-point rounding is accounted for, which is why production numerically-stable implementations avoid this ad hoc clipping entirely in favor of algebraic reformulations (log-sum-exp, computing loss directly from logits) that make the epsilon unnecessary rather than tuning it. Scientific notation also appears in code as a readable stand-in for a model's actual working precision, float32's epsilon is about `1.19e-7`, which is why a gradient check's tolerance of "around `1e-5`" in this course is calibrated to sit safely above float32's own rounding floor rather than being an arbitrary round number.

At production scale, small numerical guard constants like these are treated as part of a model's specification, not incidental code details, because changing one silently, say during a refactor or a migration to a different numeric library, can shift calibration or training dynamics in ways that are hard to trace back to their source. Mixed-precision and quantized inference make this sharper: a `1e-6` guard tuned for float32 can be entirely inadequate, or entirely unnecessary, once the same code runs in float16 or int8, so numerically-sensitive constants need to be revisited explicitly at every precision change rather than assumed to still be correct. Code review at scale for numerical code specifically looks for unexplained magic epsilons exactly like `1e-6`, since an unexplained one is either a forgotten hack or a load-bearing constant nobody has documented, and there's no way to tell which from the literal alone.

expectation.def: The long-run average outcome of a random quantity, weighting each possible value by how likely it is; written E[X].
levels: If you roll a die a huge number of times and average all the results, you'd get close to 3.5, even though the die never actually lands on 3.5. That average-over-many-tries number is the expectation, what you'd expect on average, not what happens any single time.

Expectation, written E[X], is the average value a random quantity would take if you could repeat it forever and average the results, weighting rarer outcomes less and common ones more. For a fair six-sided die, E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5; you'll never roll a 3.5, but it's the honest long-run average. In this course, a model's predicted probability p is really an estimate of E[y], the expected value of the label, since y itself is only ever exactly 0 or 1.

For a discrete random variable, E[X] = Σ x·P(X = x): multiply every possible value by its probability and add them up. For a Bernoulli outcome (0 or 1) with probability p of being 1, E[X] = 0·(1−p) + 1·p = p, which is exactly why "the model's output p" and "the expected value of the label" are the same number in logistic regression. Expectation is linear, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], always, even when X and Y are related to each other, a surprisingly powerful shortcut for computing averages of complicated sums without needing to know how the pieces interact.

For a continuous random variable, expectation is defined by an integral, E[X] = ∫ x·f(x) dx, replacing the discrete sum with area under the probability density curve, and the law of the unconscious statistician extends this to any function of X, E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)P(X=x) or ∫ g(x)f(x)dx, without needing g(X)'s own distribution. Variance is itself built from expectation, Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², and the statistical view of supervised learning, regression estimates E[y|x], classification estimates P(y=1|x), itself E[y|x] for a 0/1 label, rests on treating a model's prediction as an estimate of a conditional expectation rather than a guess at any one outcome. The sample mean is the standard estimator of E[X] from data, and by the law of large numbers it converges to the true expectation as the sample grows.

Conditional expectation, E[Y|X], is the best predictor of Y given X in the squared-error sense, and the tower property (Adam's law), E[E[Y|X]] = E[Y], and Eve's law, Var(Y) = E[Var(Y|X)] + Var(E[Y|X]), decompose a quantity's overall variability into what's explained by X and what remains, the exact formal ancestor of the bias-variance decomposition. Linearity of expectation combined with indicator random variables, writing a complicated count as a sum of 0/1 indicators and taking E of the sum, solves many otherwise painful combinatorial expectation problems by decomposition rather than brute enumeration. Expectations of unbounded or heavy-tailed quantities can fail to exist (be infinite or undefined) even when the underlying distribution is perfectly well-defined, a subtlety that trips up naive Monte Carlo estimation of quantities like ratio metrics with rare-but-extreme denominators.

In production systems, expectation is what almost every online metric actually estimates from a finite, noisy sample, an average click-through rate, an average model score, and reasoning correctly about how far a sample average can be trusted to reflect the true expectation (via its standard error, which shrinks only as 1/√n) is the difference between a metric a team can safely act on and one that's noise. Reinforcement learning and bandit systems are built almost entirely around estimating and optimizing an expected future reward under uncertainty about which action leads where, making expectation not just a descriptive statistic but the literal training objective. An open, consequential problem at scale is estimating expectations reliably for rare events, incidents, fraud, safety violations, where naive averaging over available data badly underestimates the true expectation because the events that matter most are the ones a finite sample is least likely to have captured.

correlation.def: A number from −1 to 1 measuring how closely two quantities move together in a straight-line way; it does not mean one causes the other.
levels: If ice cream sales and sunburns both go up on hot days, they're correlated, they tend to rise and fall together, even though ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Correlation is just noticing that two things move together, not explaining why.

Correlation is a number between −1 and 1 that says how closely two things tend to move together. A correlation near 1 means when one goes up, the other reliably goes up too; near −1 means when one goes up, the other reliably goes down; near 0 means they don't move together in any straight-line way. Rain and traffic incidents in this project are correlated, both tend to happen more together, but that alone doesn't prove rain causes incidents; they could both be caused by something else, or it could be a coincidence in this particular data.

The Pearson correlation coefficient, r, ranges from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 (no straight-line relationship) to 1 (perfectly together), computed from how two variables' deviations from their own means line up. `df["speed"].corr(df["flow"])` computes it directly in pandas. Correlation only captures straight-line relationships, two variables can be strongly, predictably related in a curved way and still show a correlation near 0, and it says nothing about which variable, if either, causes the other: "correlation does not imply causation" is the standard warning, and rain-and-incidents is exactly this course's own example, since traffic conditions cause both to correlate without either directly causing the other.

Formally, correlation is standardized covariance, ρ = Cov(X,Y) / (σ_X σ_Y), which is why it's unitless and bounded between −1 and 1 regardless of the original variables' scales, unlike covariance itself. Correlation is symmetric (corr(X,Y) = corr(Y,X)) and invariant to linear rescaling of either variable, but it is highly sensitive to outliers and can be driven arbitrarily close to 0 by a nonlinear relationship (a U-shape, say) that is nonetheless perfectly predictable, which is why a scatter plot alongside the number, not the number alone, is standard practice. Establishing causation instead of mere correlation generally requires either a randomized experiment (random assignment breaks the link between a treatment and any confounding variable) or careful causal-inference machinery (controlling for confounders, instrumental variables) applied to observational data like PeMS's.

Spurious correlation is a real, recurring trap, especially in time series, where two unrelated series that both trend or both have seasonal cycles can show high correlation purely from sharing that structure, not from any real relationship, which is why correlating trend-and-seasonality-heavy traffic series requires detrending or differencing first, not raw correlation on levels. Partial correlation, correlation between two variables after statistically removing a third variable's shared influence, is the standard tool for asking "are X and Y related once we account for Z," often the actually interesting question when confounding is suspected. Autocorrelation, a variable's correlation with a lagged version of itself, is a distinct but related concept central to this course's time-series work, since it determines the effective sample size and why the bootstrap must resample whole days rather than individual rows.

In production analytics, correlation is used constantly as a cheap first-pass signal, which features correlate with a target, which metrics move together in a dashboard, precisely because it's fast to compute at scale, but teams that stop at correlation for decisions that require causal claims (does this feature actually improve outcomes, or does it just correlate with users who were already going to succeed) make a well-known and costly class of mistakes. Causal inference infrastructure (uplift modeling, instrumental variables, quasi-experiments) exists specifically to go beyond correlation when a real decision, a product change, an intervention, is on the line and a true randomized experiment isn't feasible. An open, recurring engineering discipline is distinguishing, in a report or dashboard, a correlational finding clearly labeled as such from a causal one, since the two get conflated by readers far more often than by the analysts who computed them.

p-value.def: The probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if nothing real were going on; small does not mean "true," and large does not mean "false."
levels: Imagine flipping a coin ten times and getting nine heads. A p-value asks: "if this coin were actually fair, how surprising would nine-out-of-ten heads be?" A tiny p-value means "very surprising if nothing unusual were happening," which makes you suspect the coin isn't fair after all.

A hypothesis test starts by assuming nothing interesting is going on, called the null hypothesis, like "rain doesn't actually affect traffic speed." The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least as big as the one you actually measured, if that boring null hypothesis were true. A small p-value (often under 0.05 by convention) means your result would be surprising if nothing were really going on, which is evidence, not proof, against the null hypothesis.

p-value = P(a result at least this extreme | the null hypothesis is true): it measures how surprising the observed data is under a specific "nothing's happening" assumption, not the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true, and not the probability your finding is real. A common way to compute one without a formula: simulate the null hypothesis many times (shuffle which days had rain, say), recompute the statistic each time, and count what fraction of simulated results are at least as extreme as the real one, that fraction is the p-value. A small p-value is evidence against the null, but "statistically significant" (a small p-value) is not the same as "practically important": with enough data, a genuinely tiny, meaningless difference can still produce a small p-value.

Formally, a hypothesis test fixes a significance level α (commonly 0.05) in advance and rejects the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below it, which controls the long-run rate of a type 1 error, wrongly rejecting a true null, at α, at the cost of a type 2 error rate (failing to detect a real effect) that depends on the true effect size and the sample size (its complement is called power). The p-value is famously widely misinterpreted even by researchers: it is not the probability the null hypothesis is true, not the probability the result is due to chance, and not a measure of effect size, three distinct claims a single number cannot answer. Running many hypothesis tests and reporting only the significant ones (multiple comparisons, p-hacking) inflates the true false-positive rate far above the nominal α, which is why serious analyses correct for the number of tests performed or report effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside, not instead of, a bare p-value.

The replication crisis in several fields is substantially attributed to p-value misuse: treating p < 0.05 as a bright line for truth, reporting whichever of many analyses happened to cross it, and failing to distinguish statistical from practical significance, which is why modern statistical practice increasingly emphasizes effect sizes, confidence or credible intervals, and pre-registered analysis plans over p-values as the primary decision criterion. Simulation-based hypothesis testing (permutation tests, the bootstrap) generalizes cleanly to complicated statistics and dependent data, like this course's block-permutation test for a difference in medians across whole days, where a classical formula-based test's assumptions (independence, normality) don't hold. A Bayesian alternative reframes the whole question, computing a posterior probability that an effect exists or its size, rather than a p-value against a fixed null, which many statisticians argue answers the question people actually want a p-value to answer.

At production scale, A/B testing infrastructure runs thousands of hypothesis tests continuously, making multiple-comparisons correction, sequential testing (peeking at results before a test is "done" inflates false positives unless the test is explicitly designed to allow it), and pre-specified success metrics standard engineering requirements, not statistical nice-to-haves, because an uncorrected pipeline at that volume manufactures "significant" findings by chance alone. Modern experimentation platforms increasingly use Bayesian or always-valid sequential methods specifically to let teams check results early without invalidating the statistics, trading some classical-test purity for practical usability at scale. An open, recurring organizational problem is p-value literacy itself: building dashboards and review processes that make correct interpretation ("this is evidence against the null, not proof of anything") the default reading, since the misinterpretation is so natural that guarding against it takes deliberate design.

subscript.def: A small number or letter written after a variable, like x₁ or wᵢ, that says which item in a list you mean; x₁ is the first item, x₂ the second, xᵢ a generic, unspecified one.
levels: If you have a row of toy boxes and want to talk about just the third one without pointing, you could call it "box number 3." A subscript is exactly that: a small number stuck onto a name to say which one you mean, so x₃ means "the third x," not "x times 3."

A subscript is the small number or letter written just after and below a variable's name, and it's a label for "which one," not a multiplication. If x is a list of five speeds, x₁ is the first speed in the list, x₂ is the second, and so on up to x₅, the fifth. When a formula uses a letter like i or j as a subscript instead of a specific number, xᵢ, it means "a generic item, whichever one we're currently talking about," which lets one short formula describe every item in the list at once instead of writing five separate ones.

For a list (vector) x with n entries, x₁ through xₙ name its individual numbers in order, and xᵢ is shorthand for "the i-th one" when a formula needs to talk about an arbitrary entry rather than a specific one. This is what lets x·w = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + … + xₙwₙ be written compactly as Σᵢ xᵢwᵢ: the subscript i ranges over every position, and the formula describes the pattern once instead of writing it out n times. A second subscript, as in Xᵢⱼ for a matrix, adds a second "which one": i picks the row, j the column, so X₂₃ is the number in row 2, column 3. In code, this becomes ordinary indexing: `x[0]` is x₁ in math notation (code counts from 0, math notation here counts from 1), and `X[1, 2]` is X₂₃ under the same off-by-one shift.

Subscript notation is how formulas stay compact under summation, Σ, and matrix notation: a formula written with explicit subscripts, like the entropy formula H = −Σᵢ pᵢ log(pᵢ), generalizes automatically to any number of outcomes, two, six, or six hundred, without being rewritten, the entire point of using indices instead of writing out every term. Nested or double subscripts (xᵢⱼ, or a station's speed at time t written x_{s,t}) pack more than one "which one" into a single symbol, and getting the order right, which index is the row and which the column, or which the station and which the time step, matters enormously once code has to translate the notation into an actual array shape. Subscripts also distinguish training-time notation from code cleanly: a paper's xᵢ for "the i-th training example" corresponds to a specific row of a numpy array, `X[i]`, and confusing "index into the dataset" with "index into a single feature vector" is a common source of misreading a formula.

Index notation generalizes to tensors with three or more subscripts (a value at a given batch, time step and station, x_{b,t,s}), and Einstein summation convention drops the explicit Σ entirely, treating any subscript repeated across two terms in the same expression as implicitly summed over, a real notational efficiency and a common source of confusion for anyone reading such an expression for the first time without knowing the convention is in play. Careful papers distinguish a free subscript (one that appears in the result, describing which output entry a formula defines) from a bound or dummy subscript (one only used internally for summation, like i in Σᵢ, whose specific letter is arbitrary), a distinction that matters for correctly reading and re-deriving an unfamiliar equation. `einsum` in numpy and PyTorch implements this convention directly in code, letting a tensor contraction be written almost exactly as its subscript notation, at some cost to a reader unfamiliar with the convention.

At production scale, subscript-heavy paper notation is precisely what gets translated into named tensor dimensions and shape-checked code, because an off-by-one or transposed subscript in a hand-implemented formula is a classic, hard-to-catch bug that produces a plausible-looking but wrong result rather than a crash. Tools for named tensor axes, rather than positional subscripts alone, are an active area specifically because bare numeric subscripts don't scale to production code with many interacting dimensions, batch, time, station, channel, where a reader benefits far more from a name than a letter's position in the alphabet. The broader engineering lesson mirrors the one for Σ and σ: subscript notation is efficient for a paper's author and a real cost for everyone translating or maintaining the code built from it, which is why production code favors verbose indexing over literal transcription of a paper's index gymnastics.

law-of-large-numbers.def: The law of large numbers says an average settles down toward the true value as you collect more data; the central limit theorem says that average's own error shrinks and starts looking normally distributed as it does.
levels: If you flip a coin just four times, you might get all heads, that happens sometimes. But if you flip it a thousand times, the fraction of heads gets very, very close to one half. The law of large numbers is just that: the more times you try something, the closer your average gets to the truth.

The law of large numbers says that as you collect more and more data and average it, that average gets closer and closer to the true underlying value, wobbling around it less and less. Flip a fair coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads (70%); flip it 10,000 times and you'll almost certainly land very close to 50%. The central limit theorem adds a second fact: not only does the average settle down, but the shape of how wrong it tends to be, across many repeated batches of data, starts looking like the familiar bell curve, the normal distribution, no matter what the original data looked like.

The law of large numbers: as sample size n grows, a sample average converges to the true expectation E[X]. The central limit theorem goes further: for large n, a sample average's own sampling error is approximately normally distributed, centered at the truth, with a spread (standard error) that shrinks proportionally to 1/√n, so quadrupling your data only cuts typical error in half, not to a quarter.
