elbow-method.def: Two ways to pick k, the number of clusters: the elbow method looks for diminishing returns; the silhouette score measures how well-separated the clusters actually are.
levels: If you keep adding more piles to sort your buttons into, each new pile helps a little less than the last one. The elbow method watches for the exact spot where adding piles stops being worth it. The silhouette score is a different check: it asks whether each button really belongs in its own pile more than any other.

Both are ways to answer 'how many clusters (k) should I use?' when running k-means. For the elbow method, you run k-means for several values of k and plot how much total error is left at each one; the error keeps dropping as k grows, but usually there's a bend, an elbow, where it stops dropping quickly, and that bend is a reasonable choice for k. The silhouette score instead checks, for each point, whether it sits closer to its own cluster's other points than to the nearest other cluster; scores near 1 mean clean, well-separated clusters, and scores near 0 or negative mean the point is on a fuzzy boundary or in the wrong cluster.

The elbow method plots k-means's inertia (the total squared distance from each point to its cluster's center) against k, then looks for where the curve bends from steep to flat. The silhouette score for one point is (b − a)/max(a, b), where a is its average distance to points in its own cluster and b is its average distance to points in the nearest other cluster; `sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score(X, labels)` averages this over every point, and the k with the highest average silhouette is often preferred over a subjective elbow read. Neither method gives one obviously correct k; both are heuristics meant to be checked against whether the resulting clusters actually make sense.

The elbow method is informal because 'the bend' is a visual judgment call with no precise definition, which is exactly why the silhouette score, a real number rather than a shape to eyeball, is often preferred for automating the choice. Silhouette scoring has its own limitation: it implicitly favors compact, well-separated, roughly spherical clusters, the same assumption k-means itself makes, so it will systematically undervalue a genuinely good clustering with an elongated or irregular shape, where a density-based method like DBSCAN can outperform k-means despite a lower silhouette score. Both methods only use the feature space itself, with no notion of whether the resulting clusters are useful for anything, which is why checking clusters against something meaningful, like distinct station types, matters more than trusting whichever k scores best.

Beyond elbow and silhouette, several other internal validity indices exist (Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin), none uniformly best; a practitioner's real defense against overfitting the choice of k to a single index is checking stability across several random initializations and subsamples. A common mistake is running the elbow or silhouette computation on unscaled features, since both inertia and silhouette are built entirely out of distances, and an unscaled feature with a much larger numeric range will dominate the clustering and the resulting index the same way it dominates k-NN. At larger k, silhouette scoring becomes expensive, since it needs pairwise distances between every point, an O(n²) cost that forces subsampling on large datasets.

In production clustering systems, choosing k is rarely left to an automated index alone; teams pair a quantitative signal like silhouette score with a qualitative review, someone who understands the domain looking at what each cluster actually contains, because an index optimized in isolation can produce clusters that are statistically clean but operationally meaningless. At scale, computing exact silhouette scores is often infeasible, so approximate or sampled estimates substitute, trading precision for tractability on millions of rows. An open practical tension is that the 'right' k for a business use case often does not match the k an elbow or silhouette score would recommend, and reconciling the two is a routine part of applying clustering in practice.

dbscan.def: Two clustering methods needing no k ahead of time: DBSCAN groups by density, marking sparse points noise; hierarchical clustering builds a tree of merges, cuttable anywhere.
levels: Instead of deciding ahead of time how many piles to make, DBSCAN just groups things that are crowded close together and calls anything left over 'doesn't belong anywhere.' Hierarchical clustering is different: it keeps merging the two closest piles into one bigger pile, over and over, until everything is one pile, and you can stop it early wherever you like.

DBSCAN groups points that are packed closely together into a cluster and marks points sitting alone in sparse areas as noise, without ever being told how many clusters to make, unlike k-means. Hierarchical clustering instead starts with every point as its own tiny cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters into one, building up a tree called a dendrogram; cutting that tree at different heights gives different numbers of clusters, so you can explore several groupings from one run instead of rerunning the algorithm.

DBSCAN needs two settings: `eps`, how close two points must be to count as neighbors, and `min_samples`, how many neighbors a point needs to be considered 'core' and start a cluster; points that are neither core nor close to a core point get labeled −1, meaning noise. `sklearn.cluster.DBSCAN(eps=..., min_samples=...).fit(X)` runs it. Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering builds a dendrogram, a tree diagram where the height of each merge shows how far apart the two groups were when they joined; cutting the tree at a chosen height (or asking for a chosen number of clusters) reads off the actual groups. DBSCAN's strength is finding oddly shaped clusters and flagging outliers automatically; hierarchical clustering's strength is showing the whole nested structure at once instead of committing to one k.

DBSCAN's density-based definition means it makes no assumption that clusters are round or similarly sized, unlike k-means, which is why it can find a long, curving cluster of stations along a winding freeway that k-means would incorrectly split into several round pieces; its cost is that `eps` and `min_samples` are not intuitive to set, and a bad choice can merge everything into one cluster or mark almost everything as noise. Hierarchical clustering's merge rule, called the linkage (single, complete, average, or Ward), changes what 'closest' means between two whole clusters, and the choice matters: single linkage can chain together a long stretch of points through a thin bridge, while Ward linkage tends to produce more balanced, compact clusters, closer in spirit to k-means. Both methods scale worse than k-means on large data, since DBSCAN needs a neighbor search for every point and naive hierarchical clustering is O(n²) or worse.

DBSCAN's sensitivity to a single global `eps` is a real limitation when clusters at different densities exist in the same dataset, since one `eps` cannot serve both well; HDBSCAN generalizes DBSCAN to handle varying density by building a hierarchy of DBSCAN-like clusterings and extracting the most stable clusters from it. For hierarchical clustering, the dendrogram's shape itself is diagnostic: a few very tall, well-separated merges near the top suggest a genuinely small number of natural clusters, while gradual merging with no clear tall gaps suggests the data does not have strongly separated groups at all. Both algorithms, unlike k-means, produce deterministic results given the same data and settings, since neither depends on a random initialization.

At production scale, DBSCAN and classical hierarchical clustering are both used sparingly on very large datasets because of their scaling costs; approximate nearest-neighbor structures make density-based clustering on millions of points tractable, and hierarchical clustering at scale typically uses a coarser sample rather than every point. Density-based clustering remains popular in anomaly and fault detection pipelines precisely because 'noise' maps naturally onto 'this reading doesn't look like anything we've seen before.' An open tension across both methods is that neither gives a probability for its cluster assignments, so production systems needing calibrated uncertainty typically layer a probabilistic model, a Gaussian mixture, on top instead.

isolation-forest.def: An anomaly detector that builds random decision trees and flags a point as unusual if it takes very few splits to isolate it from everything else.
levels: Imagine playing twenty questions to separate one toy from a whole toybox. A weird, unusual toy is easy to separate in just a couple of questions, while a normal one takes lots of questions to tell apart from all its lookalikes. An isolation forest is a computer doing exactly that trick over and over to find the weird ones.

An isolation forest builds many random trees that split the data on random features at random thresholds, over and over, until every point is alone in its own little group. A normal point, surrounded by lots of similar points, takes many splits to isolate, while an unusual, outlier point stands out and gets isolated in just a few splits. Averaging how many splits it took across many random trees gives each point an anomaly score.

`sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest(n_estimators=..., contamination=...).fit(X)` builds many random trees, each splitting on a randomly chosen feature at a randomly chosen threshold; `.decision_function(X)` or `.predict(X)` (returning −1 for anomalies) scores each row by its average path length, how many splits it took to isolate it, across all trees. `contamination` sets roughly what fraction of the data you expect to be anomalous. It works well for spotting a detector stuck at an impossible reading, since a wildly wrong value tends to separate from everything else in very few splits, without needing labeled examples of what 'broken' looks like.

The key insight is structural rather than distance-based: instead of measuring how far a point is from its neighbors, isolation forest measures how easy it is to separate under random partitioning, which scales much better to high dimensions and large datasets, since it never needs pairwise distances at all. Because splits are random rather than optimized, isolation forest trees are cheap to build, and the ensemble average over many random trees is what makes the anomaly score stable despite each individual tree being close to arbitrary. It tends to work best for point anomalies, single rows far from everything else, and less well for contextual anomalies, a reading only unusual given the time of day, unless that context is explicitly engineered into the input features.

Isolation forest's random-split construction means its anomaly score is only meaningful relative to the specific feature set and scaling used to build it, so two runs on differently engineered feature sets for the same rows can flag different points as anomalous. `contamination` is a genuinely awkward hyperparameter, since it asks the practitioner to already know roughly what fraction of the data is anomalous, often exactly the unknown quantity anomaly detection is meant to discover; a common workaround is treating the raw score's distribution as the object of interest and setting a threshold by inspection instead. Compared to a reconstruction-error-based method like an autoencoder, isolation forest needs no training signal beyond the raw features, a cheap, robust first pass, though it captures a narrower notion of 'unusual' than a learned reconstruction model can.

In production anomaly-detection pipelines, isolation forest is a common first line of defense precisely because it needs no labeled anomalies, trains fast even on large feature sets, and degrades gracefully as the definition of 'unusual' drifts over time. For sensor networks specifically, isolation forest and similar unsupervised detectors are often run continuously as a health-monitoring layer ahead of the actual forecasting model, flagging suspect detector-days before they can poison training data. The open engineering problem is less the algorithm and more the feedback loop: without labeled ground truth on which flagged points were genuinely anomalous, a team has limited ability to measure whether the detector's precision is actually improving over time.

eigenvector.def: A direction that a matrix only stretches, never rotates (the eigenvector), and the amount it stretches by (the eigenvalue); PCA's principal components are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix.
levels: Imagine a machine that pushes every arrow in a picture in some new direction — except for a few special arrows that it only makes longer or shorter, without turning them at all. Those special directions are eigenvectors, and how much longer or shorter the machine makes them is the eigenvalue.

When you multiply a matrix by most vectors, the result points in a new direction. But for a special few directions, called eigenvectors, multiplying by the matrix only stretches or shrinks the vector, it keeps pointing the same way. The number telling you how much it stretched or shrank is the eigenvalue for that direction. PCA works by finding a dataset's eigenvectors, the directions where the data spreads out the most, and using the biggest ones as new, simplified axes.

For a square matrix A, a vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ if Av = λv, meaning multiplying v by A gives back the same direction v, just scaled by λ. In PCA, A is the covariance matrix of the (usually standardized) features; its eigenvectors are the principal components, the new axes, and each one's eigenvalue tells you how much of the data's total variance that axis captures. `numpy.linalg.eig(cov_matrix)` computes both directly, though `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` handles this internally and hands you `.components_` and `.explained_variance_ratio_` without you ever calling `eig` yourself.

For a real, symmetric matrix like a covariance matrix, the eigenvectors are guaranteed to be mutually orthogonal and the eigenvalues are guaranteed to be real and non-negative, which is exactly why PCA's principal components come out as a clean, uncorrelated set of new axes rather than an arbitrary jumble. Sorting the eigenvectors by their eigenvalues from largest to smallest and keeping only the top few is precisely what 'keep the components that explain the most variance' means in practice; an eigenvalue near zero means that direction barely varies in the data and can usually be dropped with little information lost. Computing eigenvectors directly from a covariance matrix is numerically less stable than computing them via the singular value decomposition of the original data matrix, which is why production PCA implementations use SVD internally rather than the textbook eigendecomposition.

Eigenvectors and eigenvalues generalize well beyond PCA: they characterize the long-run behavior of any repeated linear transformation, which is why they show up in Markov chain steady states, in graph spectral clustering (the eigenvectors of a graph's Laplacian matrix), and in analyzing whether a repeated update rule converges or blows up, since a transformation with an eigenvalue greater than 1 in some direction amplifies error along that direction every time it is applied. For a non-symmetric matrix, eigenvalues can be complex numbers and eigenvectors are not guaranteed to be orthogonal, which is why PCA specifically relies on the covariance matrix being symmetric. A common misconception is treating a small eigenvalue as automatically unimportant; if the corresponding direction happens to carry the exact signal a downstream task cares about, discarding it because it has low variance can throw away the most useful information.

At production scale, eigendecomposition and its faster relative, randomized SVD, are workhorse tools well beyond PCA proper: they underlie whitening transformations, spectral clustering, and diagnostics that probe what structure a trained neural network's internal representations have actually learned. For very large matrices, computing all eigenvectors exactly is prohibitively expensive, so production systems use iterative methods that approximate only the top few, which is all most applications actually need. An open, actively used engineering technique is truncated or randomized eigendecomposition tuned to a matrix's structure, trading exactness for the ability to run this classical linear-algebra tool on datasets far larger than a naive implementation could ever handle.

t-sne.def: Two techniques that squeeze high-dimensional data down to two or three dimensions for a plot, preserving which points were close neighbors rather than the overall geometry PCA preserves.
levels: Imagine you have a huge pile of photos and want to lay them out on one table so that photos of similar things end up near each other. t-SNE and UMAP are two different ways a computer does exactly that, so you can actually look at the pile and see the groups.

t-SNE and UMAP are both ways to turn data with many features into just two numbers per row, so you can plot it and see it with your own eyes. Unlike PCA, which tries to preserve the overall spread of the data, t-SNE and UMAP focus on keeping points that were close together in the original high-dimensional space close together in the 2D picture, even if that distorts the overall shape. They're mainly used for looking at data, not as an input to another model, since the 2D positions they produce don't mean anything mathematically the way PCA's components do.

`sklearn.manifold.TSNE(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)` and the separate `umap-learn` package's `UMAP(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)` both take a high-dimensional feature matrix and return 2D coordinates for plotting. Both work by modeling which points are 'neighbors' in the original space and then arranging points in 2D so that neighbor relationships are preserved as well as possible, which is why they're good at revealing clusters that PCA's straight-line projection can miss. Neither preserves distances between far-apart points meaningfully, so two clusters that look far apart in a plot are not necessarily far apart in the real data, only their local neighborhoods were kept intact.

Both methods build a graph or probability distribution over which points are neighbors in the high-dimensional space, then optimize a 2D layout so the same neighbor relationships hold approximately, but their objectives differ: t-SNE minimizes the KL divergence between the high- and low-dimensional neighbor distributions, using a heavy-tailed distribution in the low-dimensional space to prevent crowding, while UMAP builds on a more explicit topological framework and is generally faster and better at preserving some global structure alongside local neighborhoods. Both are sensitive to hyperparameters, t-SNE's perplexity and UMAP's number of neighbors, that effectively set the scale of 'local' being preserved, and different settings on the same data can produce visibly different-looking cluster shapes. Because both are nonlinear and non-deterministic, they should never be used to feed features into another model, only PCA and similar linear or exactly-invertible methods are safe for that.

A well-known trap with t-SNE specifically is that cluster sizes and inter-cluster distances in the resulting plot are not meaningful even qualitatively, a big-looking cluster in the embedding is not necessarily a big cluster in the real data, one of the most common misinterpretations of these plots in applied work; UMAP is somewhat less prone to this but not immune. Practitioners increasingly prefer UMAP over t-SNE for exploratory work because it scales better to larger datasets and tends to preserve more global structure. Neither method comes with the kind of principled 'how many components should I keep, and how much variance did I lose' accounting that PCA provides, since neither is trying to preserve variance in the first place.

At production scale, t-SNE and UMAP remain firmly visualization and exploratory-analysis tools, used to sanity-check what a learned embedding space actually looks like, rather than as components inside a production model itself. UMAP in particular has found a secondary production role as a fast, approximate dimensionality-reduction preprocessing step ahead of a downstream clustering algorithm, since its speed and reasonable structure-preservation make it usable at a scale t-SNE cannot reach. An open frontier is building embedding visualization tools that scale interactively to millions of points in real time, pushing research toward GPU-accelerated and incremental variants of both.

em.def: An algorithm for fitting a model with hidden, unobserved structure by alternating between guessing the hidden values and refitting the model, until it stops improving.
levels: Imagine sorting jellybeans into flavor groups by taste alone, but you can't be totally sure which flavor each one is. EM is a strategy: guess your best sorting, then use that guess to get better at telling flavors apart, then re-sort with your new skill, and repeat until your guesses stop changing.

Expectation-maximization (EM) is a way to fit a model when some important information is hidden, like which of several groups a data point actually belongs to. It alternates between two steps: the 'expectation' step guesses how likely each point is to belong to each hidden group given the current model, and the 'maximization' step refits the model using those guessed probabilities as if they were real. Repeating these two steps, guess then refit, gradually improves both the guesses and the model until they stop changing much.

For a Gaussian mixture model with k hidden groups, the E-step computes, for each point, the probability it belongs to each group given the current group means and spreads; the M-step then recomputes each group's mean, spread and size using those probabilities as weights, instead of hard assignments. `sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture(n_components=k).fit(X)` runs EM under the hood and returns `.means_`, `.covariances_` and `.predict_proba(X)` for the soft group memberships. k-means is a simplified, 'hard-assignment' special case of EM, where every point is forced fully into its single nearest group instead of getting a probability spread across several.

EM is provably guaranteed to never make the data's likelihood under the model worse at each iteration, though it is only guaranteed to reach a local maximum, not the global best fit, which is why EM for a Gaussian mixture is typically run from several random starting points and the best result kept. The E-step's 'soft' probabilistic group assignments are what distinguish EM from k-means's hard, all-or-nothing assignments, and this is exactly what lets a Gaussian mixture represent overlapping groups, a point genuinely ambiguous between two clusters, in a way k-means structurally cannot. EM generalizes far beyond Gaussian mixtures: it is the standard fitting algorithm whenever a model has a natural notion of hidden or latent variables, hidden Markov model states and missing-data imputation among them, all sharing the same alternate-and-refit structure.

k-means can be derived formally as the limit of EM for a Gaussian mixture as each group's variance shrinks toward zero, since the soft group-membership probabilities collapse to a hard 0-or-1 assignment to whichever group's center is nearest, a clean illustration of a simpler, faster algorithm being a special case of a more general, more expensive one. EM's local-maximum guarantee is weaker than it sounds in high dimensions or with many hidden groups, since the number of genuinely different local optima grows quickly, and initialization strategy matters as much as the algorithm itself for getting a usable fit. A subtlety practitioners get wrong: EM's likelihood is guaranteed non-decreasing only on the training data it was fit on, which says nothing about whether the fitted mixture generalizes, so model selection (how many hidden groups k) still needs a held-out check, commonly via the Bayesian information criterion, not just the training likelihood.

EM remains foundational infrastructure well beyond explicit Gaussian mixtures: variational inference, the workhorse behind training variational autoencoders and many Bayesian deep learning methods, is a direct generalization of EM's alternate-and-refit structure to cases where the E-step itself cannot be computed exactly. In production systems, EM-based mixture models are still used for genuinely interpretable latent-state problems, like inferring discrete traffic regimes from continuous sensor readings, where a black-box neural model would give comparable accuracy but no interpretable notion of 'which regime is this station in right now.' An open research thread is scaling EM's guarantees, well understood for simple mixture models, to the much more complex latent-variable structures used in modern generative models.

var.def: ARIMA extended to several time series at once, where each series is predicted from its own recent past and every other series' recent past together.
levels: ARIMA guesses tomorrow's number from just one thing's own past. VAR is the same idea but for a whole group of things at once, where each one's guess can use everybody's recent past, not just its own.

A vector autoregression (VAR) predicts several time series together instead of one at a time. Each series' next value is predicted from a mix of its own recent past values and every other series' recent past values, so a VAR modeling three nearby stations' speeds lets each station's forecast be pulled by what its neighbors were doing too, not just its own history.

A VAR(p) model writes each series' next value as a linear combination of the last p values of every series in the group, including itself: for stations A and B, speedA(t) depends on speedA(t−1)...speedA(t−p) and speedB(t−1)...speedB(t−p) together, with its own set of learned weights. `statsmodels.tsa.api.VAR(data).fit(p)` fits it on a table with one column per series. It's the classical, linear way to capture the kind of cross-station influence this course's graph and neighbor-mixing models learn nonlinearly instead.

VAR generalizes ARIMA from one series to several by stacking their lag equations together into a matrix system, and its coefficients are directly interpretable, a large weight on station B's lagged speed in station A's equation says B genuinely helps predict A, which single-series ARIMA cannot express at all. Fitting a VAR requires choosing a lag order p (often by AIC or BIC, the same criteria ARIMA uses) and, like ARIMA, works best on stationary series, so the same differencing and deseasonalizing steps apply. The number of parameters grows with the square of the number of series, since every series gets its own weights on every other series' lags, which is exactly why VAR does not scale to a hundred stations the way a global LightGBM or graph model does.

VAR's quadratic parameter growth is its central practical limitation: with a hundred stations and even a modest lag order, the coefficients to estimate can exceed what the available data can reliably fit, producing an overfit, unstable model, exactly the scaling wall that motivated moving toward a single global model that shares parameters across stations instead of estimating a separate weight for every pair. Structural VAR extends plain VAR with assumptions about the causal ordering between series, letting practitioners ask counterfactual questions a plain VAR's coefficients alone cannot answer. VAR is also the classical entry point into state-space and Kalman-filter thinking, since a VAR model can be rewritten exactly as a linear state-space system.

At production scale, plain VAR is rarely deployed directly for anything beyond a handful of series, since its quadratic parameter growth and its assumption of a fixed, dense set of pairwise linear relationships do not hold up against the sparsity, one station really only interacts with its true road-network neighbors, that a graph-structured model can encode explicitly and VAR cannot. VAR nonetheless remains a valuable diagnostic and baseline tool, useful for sanity-checking whether a more complex learned model is actually capturing real cross-series structure or just overfitting noise a simple linear model would also pick up. An open research thread is sparse or regularized VAR, imposing a graph-like sparsity pattern on which series influence which others, bridging classical VAR toward the same neighbor-structure assumption a graph model encodes directly.

stl.def: A way to split a time series into trend, seasonal and leftover pieces, robust to outliers and able to handle more than one seasonal cycle at once.
levels: Imagine taking a wiggly line and pulling it apart into three simpler lines: one that shows the slow overall direction, one that shows the repeating daily up-and-down, and one that's just whatever is left over and unexplained. STL is a way of doing exactly that split.

STL stands for 'seasonal and trend decomposition using LOESS,' a smoothing technique; it takes a time series, like a station's speed over a month, and splits it into three parts you can look at separately: the slow-moving trend, the repeating seasonal pattern (like the daily rush-hour cycle), and the leftover residual that neither of those explains. It's especially good at handling a series with more than one repeating cycle at once, like both a daily and a weekly pattern, and it isn't thrown off by a handful of unusual days the way a simpler decomposition can be.

`statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL(series, period=288).fit()` (288 being the number of five-minute slots in a day) returns `.trend`, `.seasonal` and `.resid` components that add back up to the original series. Unlike a simple moving-average decomposition, STL fits the trend and seasonal pieces with a smoother called LOESS (locally weighted regression), which makes it robust to outliers, a single crash day won't distort the whole trend estimate, and flexible enough to let the seasonal shape itself change slowly over the series. Plotting all three components stacked together is the standard first look at a new series.

STL's core mechanism, iterating between LOESS-smoothed trend and seasonal fits, each computed on the series with the other component removed, is what gives it both its flexibility (the seasonal component can drift gradually rather than being locked to one fixed shape) and its robustness (an inner loop downweights points with unusually large residuals so a handful of crash days don't distort the fit). It handles only one seasonal period natively per call, so a series with both daily and weekly seasonality, exactly this course's traffic data, typically needs either two chained STL passes or a multiple-seasonal variant (MSTL). STL's residual component is itself a reasonable starting point for anomaly detection, since a residual far larger than the rest, deseasonalized and detrended, is a candidate for an incident or a broken detector.

STL sits between two extremes of decomposition, a rigid, globally fixed seasonal-dummy approach that can't adapt if the seasonal pattern drifts, and a fully flexible model, like letting a neural network learn seasonality implicitly, that adapts completely but loses the clean, inspectable breakdown STL provides. Its LOESS smoothing parameters trade responsiveness against smoothness, a seasonal window too short lets STL absorb genuine anomalies into the 'seasonal' component instead of leaving them in the residual, quietly defeating the point of using STL for anomaly detection. A practitioner mistake is running STL once on a full multi-year series and treating the resulting seasonal component as fixed forever, when real seasonality, commute patterns especially, drifts slowly enough that an old decomposition can silently stop matching current conditions.

In production forecasting and monitoring systems, STL and its multiple-seasonal variants are commonly run continuously as a first-pass diagnostic layer ahead of a learned forecasting model, both to hand the model cleaner deseasonalized inputs and to generate an interpretable residual stream a separate anomaly-detection system can watch. At scale, running STL per series rather than one global decomposition is standard, since each series' seasonal shape and trend genuinely differ, which multiplies computation but is cheap enough per series to rarely be the bottleneck. An open practical question is how to keep an STL-based pipeline's estimates fresh under continuous data arrival without constantly refitting the whole historical series from scratch, which is where incremental or online decomposition variants become relevant.

direct-forecasting.def: Two ways to predict several steps ahead: direct trains a separate model per horizon; recursive trains one model and feeds its own prediction back in for the next step.
levels: If you want to guess the weather for the next three days, you could either train three separate weather-guessers, one for tomorrow, one for the day after, one for the day after that (that's direct), or train just one guesser for tomorrow and then guess again using your own guess as if it were true (that's recursive).

When a model needs to predict several steps into the future, like speed 15, 30 and 60 minutes out, there are two basic strategies. The direct strategy trains a separate model for each horizon, one model only ever asked to predict 15 minutes out, another only ever asked for 30, and so on. The recursive strategy instead trains just one model to predict one step ahead, then runs it repeatedly, feeding each prediction back in as if it were a real observation to predict the next step after that.

Direct: train model_15, model_30 and model_60 separately, each with its own target column (`y_15`, `y_30`, `y_60`) but the same input features; each model only ever has to be right about its own single horizon. Recursive: train one model to predict one step ahead (five minutes), then to get a 30-minute forecast, run it, feed its own output back in as the new 'current' value, and run it again, repeating six times. This course uses the direct strategy: recursive forecasting compounds error, since a bad five-minute guess becomes a wrong input to the next step, and that mistake keeps propagating and can grow at every step it's fed back in.

The direct strategy avoids recursive's compounding-error problem by construction, since each horizon's model is trained and evaluated against real, observed values, never against its own earlier predictions, but it pays for that by not sharing any explicit structure across horizons, and training and maintaining several separate models multiplies the operational cost. Recursive forecasting is more data-efficient and naturally extends to any horizon by just running it more times, but its errors compound multiplicatively with the horizon, since each step's input includes the accumulated error of every prior step. A third option, DirRec, combines the two: it trains a separate model per horizon like direct, but each later model also gets to use the earlier horizons' predictions as extra input features.

The bias-variance framing clarifies the tradeoff: recursive forecasting has lower variance (one model, more effective training data) but higher bias at long horizons because it's optimized for one-step error, not the multi-step error it's actually used for, while direct forecasting has each model correctly optimized for its own horizon's real loss but effectively less data per model and no mechanism sharing what one horizon learned with another. A less obvious cost of the direct strategy is horizon incoherence: since model_15, model_30 and model_60 are trained independently, nothing enforces their predictions form a sensible, mutually consistent trajectory. This course's own STNet architecture sidesteps the choice partly by predicting all three horizons from one shared model in one forward pass, sharing representation across horizons the way recursive does while still training directly against each horizon's real target the way direct does.

In production forecasting systems serving many horizons at once, the operational cost of the direct strategy, maintaining a separate model per horizon, is a real, recurring line item, part of why multi-output and multi-task architectures have become the common production compromise: closer to direct's per-horizon accuracy without direct's full multiplication of maintenance cost. Recursive forecasting nonetheless persists for very long or open-ended horizons, where training a genuinely separate direct model for every possible horizon is impractical. An open research question is hybrid strategies that dynamically decide, per series or per horizon, whether direct's independence or recursive's shared efficiency is the better tradeoff.

successive-halving.def: Hyperparameter-search methods that run many trials with a small budget each, then keep only the best-performing ones and give them a bigger budget, repeating until one trial wins.
levels: Imagine a talent show where everyone gets one minute to show off, then only the best half get invited back for a longer, five-minute round, and this repeats until only the very best is left. That's how successive halving picks good settings without wasting time on bad ones.

Successive halving starts many hyperparameter settings at once, but gives each one only a small budget, like a few rounds of training, then throws away the worse-performing half and gives the survivors a bigger budget, repeating this halve-and-extend process until one setting is left standing. Hyperband is a refinement of the same idea that also varies how aggressively it halves and how many settings it starts with, running several versions of successive halving with different tradeoffs, to hedge against picking the wrong tradeoff up front.

In this course's setting, a 'budget' is boosting rounds: successive halving might start 32 LightGBM configurations at 50 rounds each, keep the best 16 and give them 100 rounds, keep the best 8 at 200 rounds, and so on, until only a few configurations remain at a large round count. This is efficient because most bad settings reveal themselves as bad early, so spending a full training budget on them is wasted; Optuna's median pruner and its Hyperband integration implement this directly, stopping a trial early once it's clearly falling behind the median of trials at the same point. It's the mechanism behind the 'early-stopping-based methods' this phase's tuning topic mentions, distinct from a single model's own early stopping on one training run.

Successive halving has one real weakness: the choice of how aggressively to eliminate trials trades off against how much budget survivors get, and getting that tradeoff wrong can eliminate a setting that would have turned out well with a bit more budget, a false negative plain successive halving has no way to recover from. Hyperband addresses this by running several 'brackets,' each a differently tuned successive-halving schedule, and pooling their results, which provably matches the best individual bracket's performance without needing to know in advance which bracket would have been right for this specific problem. Both methods assume a trial's relative ranking early in training predicts its relative ranking later, an assumption that mostly holds for something like boosting rounds but can fail for hyperparameters whose effect only shows up much later in training.

Successive halving and Hyperband are compatible with, and often combined with, a smarter sampler like TPE or a Gaussian process for choosing which configurations to try in the first place, since halving only decides how much budget each trial gets, not which configurations are worth trying, the two problems are genuinely separable and modern tuning libraries let you mix and match a sampler with a pruner independently. The 'budget' doesn't have to be boosting rounds; it generalizes to any resource a trial can be given more or less of, training epochs, dataset subsample size, or model size. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is applying successive halving to a metric that is itself noisy at low budgets, which can eliminate a genuinely good configuration purely because its early score happened to be unlucky.

At production scale, successive-halving-based methods are core infrastructure for hyperparameter and neural architecture search, since compute is the binding constraint and eliminating clearly bad configurations early is the single biggest lever for getting more search done within a fixed budget; distributed implementations run thousands of trials in parallel, with the scheduler deciding in real time which trials survive. The research frontier includes learning the early-ranking assumption itself rather than assuming it, fitting a model of how a trial's trajectory evolves to make earlier, more confident elimination decisions. An open engineering tension is that successive halving's efficiency gains are largest when trials are cheap and numerous, at odds with the trend toward training runs so expensive that only a handful of trials are affordable at all.

kalman-filter.def: A method for tracking a hidden, changing quantity over time from noisy measurements, blending a prediction of where it should be with each new noisy reading.
levels: Imagine trying to track a rolling ball with your eyes closed, using only occasional, blurry glimpses. You'd guess where it should be based on how it was moving, then nudge your guess a little whenever you got a new blurry glimpse. A Kalman filter is a computer doing exactly that math.

A Kalman filter keeps a running estimate of something changing over time, like a station's true underlying speed, that you can only measure noisily. At each step it does two things: predicts where the quantity should be based on how it's been moving, then blends that prediction with the new noisy measurement, trusting whichever one it's more confident in. It's the classical way computers track a moving, uncertain quantity from a stream of imperfect readings, used everywhere from GPS navigation to spacecraft.

The Kalman filter maintains both an estimate of the hidden quantity and its own uncertainty about that estimate; at each new reading it computes a 'Kalman gain,' a number between 0 and 1 that decides how much weight to give the new measurement versus its own prior prediction, weighting the measurement more when the filter is unsure and less when it's already confident. `statsmodels`'s state-space module implements this under the hood for models like SARIMAX and `UnobservedComponents`, so fitting one of those is, mechanically, running a Kalman filter to estimate the hidden trend and seasonal levels from noisy observed speed readings. It only works cleanly for linear systems with Gaussian noise; nonlinear versions exist but lose the same clean guarantees.

The Kalman filter is provably the optimal linear estimator for a linear system with Gaussian noise, which is why it remains the standard tool wherever those assumptions hold reasonably well, and it operates recursively, updating its estimate with each new reading in constant time rather than needing to reprocess the whole history, well suited to real-time, streaming settings. Framed as a state-space model, the hidden quantity being tracked is the latent state, and the Kalman filter is really doing the same predict-then-correct dance a recurrent network's hidden state update performs, just with a much more constrained, linear, closed-form update rule instead of learned nonlinear gates. This is exactly the connection this course draws when it frames a GRU as 'a nonlinear state-space model.'

The classical Kalman filter assumes the system's dynamics and noise are both linear and Gaussian and, crucially, known in advance, assumptions that rarely hold exactly for something as nonlinear as traffic dynamics near a bottleneck, precisely why this course's learned sequence and graph models exist rather than a hand-specified Kalman filter; extended and unscented Kalman filters relax the linearity assumption at the cost of losing the exact optimality guarantee. Filtering and smoothing are also distinct: filtering estimates the hidden state using only past and current measurements (appropriate for real-time forecasting), while smoothing revisits the whole series afterward using future measurements too (appropriate for cleaning historical data, not for forecasting). A practitioner mistake is applying a smoothed estimate where a filtered one is required, silently leaking future information into what's meant to be a real-time forecast.

In production systems, Kalman filters and their variants remain the standard choice wherever a genuinely interpretable, real-time, low-latency state estimate is needed with a provable uncertainty bound, GPS and sensor fusion being the canonical examples, and they persist as a robust fallback or preprocessing denoising layer even in systems whose main forecasting model is a much more complex learned network. For traffic-adjacent applications, Kalman filters remain common in the sensor-fusion layer that combines noisy fixed-detector readings with noisy probe or GPS data into one best estimate of current conditions, a distinct problem from forecasting the future. An open research thread is differentiable or learned Kalman filters, keeping the classical predict-correct structure for its efficiency but learning its transition and noise models from data rather than hand-specifying them.

ordinal-classification.def: Classifying into categories that have a real order (light < moderate < heavy), penalizing being off by one category less than being off by two, unlike ordinary multiclass loss.
levels: If you're grading traffic as light, medium, or heavy, guessing 'medium' when it's really 'light' is a much smaller mistake than guessing 'heavy'. Ordinal classification is a way of teaching a model that these mistakes aren't all equally bad, the way an ordinary sorting-into-groups model would treat them.

When the categories a model is sorting into actually have an order, like light, moderate and heavy congestion, treating it as an ordinary multiclass problem throws away useful information: an ordinary softmax model treats guessing 'heavy' when the truth is 'light' as exactly as wrong as guessing 'moderate' when the truth is 'light', even though one mistake is clearly worse. Ordinal classification uses a loss function that respects the order, penalizing a prediction more the further away it lands from the true category, so a model naturally learns to prefer being off by one step over being off by two.

One simple approach: instead of one softmax over three unordered classes, train several binary classifiers, each answering 'is this at least moderate?' and 'is this at least heavy?', then combine their answers, which automatically respects the order since 'at least heavy' implies 'at least moderate.' Another approach treats the ordinal label as a number (0, 1, 2) and applies ordinary regression, then rounds the output back to the nearest category, borrowing regression's natural notion of 'how far off.' Small Python packages like `mord` implement dedicated ordinal classifiers directly, though a plain softmax trained while just being aware the classes have an order is a reasonable shortcut too.

The cumulative-link approach (used by ordinal logistic regression) models P(Y ≤ k) directly as a function of the features, using a single set of feature weights shared across all the category thresholds, more parameter-efficient than fitting a separate model per threshold and, by construction, guaranteeing the predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically ordered. A plain multiclass loss is a real modeling choice that discards genuine structure in the problem, since it optimizes for getting the exact category right rather than for minimizing how far off a wrong guess lands, which matters operationally when a 'moderate' misclassified as 'light' is materially worse for a driver than 'moderate' misclassified as 'heavy'. Evaluating an ordinal classifier also calls for ordinal-aware metrics, like a weighted kappa that penalizes larger category gaps more, rather than plain accuracy.

The choice between treating an ordinal target as classification-with-an-ordinal-loss versus as plain regression-then-rounding is really a choice about which errors matter: regression naturally penalizes distance in the underlying continuous quantity, while a genuinely ordinal classification loss penalizes distance in category rank, and these can disagree when the categories aren't evenly spaced in the underlying continuous value. Gradient-boosted trees don't have a native ordinal objective, so ordinal targets with tree ensembles are usually handled either by the cumulative-binary-classifier trick or by training a plain regression on the underlying continuous value and only discretizing at the very end, for reporting. A common mistake is picking ordinal category boundaries arbitrarily and then treating the resulting classes as if they always had equal practical importance.

In production severity-grading systems, ordinal structure shows up constantly, congestion levels, priority tiers, risk grades, and treating them with plain multiclass tooling is a common, quietly costly mistake, since a monitoring dashboard built on plain accuracy will not surface that a model's errors have gotten systematically worse (off by two categories instead of one) even while raw accuracy looks stable. Teams that get this right typically report an ordinal-aware metric like weighted kappa alongside accuracy, specifically so a regression in error severity, not just error rate, gets caught. An open, still-debated design question is whether to build a dedicated ordinal model at all or simply train the best possible continuous regression and only ever discretize into categories at the reporting layer.

rolling-origin-evaluation.def: Testing a forecasting model by repeatedly moving the train/test split forward in time, so every fold trains only on the past and tests only on what comes after it.
levels: Imagine practicing guessing tomorrow's weather using only what you knew up to today, then moving forward a day and doing it again, over and over. That's rolling-origin evaluation: it never lets you peek at the future, and it checks you many times, not just once.

Rolling-origin evaluation tests a forecasting model the way it will actually be used: train on everything up to some date, test on what comes right after, then move the split forward and repeat, so you get several honest test scores from different points in time instead of just one. It's called 'rolling' because the origin, the point where training stops and testing starts, rolls forward through the data with each fold, and it's the time-series version of the ordinary cross-validation used for earlier, non-time-series models.

`sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)` implements this directly: each of its 5 folds trains only on data before that fold's test window and tests only on data after it, unlike ordinary k-fold cross-validation, which would shuffle rows randomly and let a model train on future data to predict the past, a leak. Reporting the spread of scores across the rolling-origin folds, not just their average, tells you whether a model's skill is consistent over time or whether it happens to do well on some periods and badly on others. This is what this course means whenever it mentions 'the chronological validation split' or a model being tuned 'on the rolling-origin folds.'

Rolling-origin evaluation directly simulates the deployment reality of a periodically retrained forecasting system: each fold's train/test boundary stands in for a real retraining date, and the honest test score at each fold reflects what the model would actually have achieved if deployed and used starting right there, which ordinary shuffled cross-validation cannot approximate at all for temporally dependent data. There's a real design choice in how folds are constructed: an expanding window keeps all past data in every successive fold's training set, while a sliding window keeps a fixed-size training window that moves forward, and the choice matters for whether a model's apparent improvement over folds reflects genuinely more informative recent data or just more data overall. A gap between the end of a training window and the start of its test window (this course's 'one-day gap') is often inserted deliberately, to prevent a subtle leak where a rolling-window feature near the boundary accidentally uses information from just inside the test period.

Rolling-origin evaluation with multiple folds is more expensive to run than a single fixed split, since it means retraining the model once per fold, which for an expensive model can make a full evaluation prohibitively slow, pushing practitioners toward fewer folds or a single, carefully chosen split, accepting a noisier estimate for tractable compute. When rolling-origin evaluation is also used to select hyperparameters, the same selection-bias problem that plain cross-validation has applies here too, and the honest fix is the same: a final held-out test period that was never touched during tuning, evaluated only once. A subtlety specific to time series: later folds necessarily contain more recent, often more representative, data of current conditions, so a model's score naturally tends to look different on later folds than earlier ones, and averaging blindly without looking at the trend in per-fold scores can hide a model that is systematically improving, or degrading, as the series goes on.

In production forecasting systems, rolling-origin evaluation is the offline analogue of backtesting a strategy against history, and it has to be designed to match the actual production retraining cadence exactly, evaluating with folds spaced a day apart when the real system retrains monthly gives a misleadingly optimistic picture of how fresh the model actually is between real retraining events. At scale, rolling-origin evaluation across many series multiplies the already-substantial compute cost of multiple folds by the number of series, which is why production teams often evaluate a representative sample with full rigor and monitor the rest with cheaper, single-split checks. An open, still-recurring practical failure is a rolling-origin evaluation that looks rigorous but silently uses a feature-engineering pipeline fit once on the full dataset rather than refit per fold, which reintroduces exactly the future-leaking the whole design was meant to prevent.

mase.def: Forecast-error metrics divided by a naive baseline's error, so a score below 1 means the model beats naive guessing and scores are comparable across very different series.
levels: Imagine grading a guess not by how far off it was, but by how much better it was than the laziest possible guess, like saying 'tomorrow will be the same as today.' MASE and RMSSE are scores built exactly that way, so a small station and a huge station can be compared fairly.

MASE (mean absolute scaled error) and RMSSE (root mean squared scaled error) both take a normal error measurement and divide it by how wrong a naive forecast, usually just repeating the last known value, would have been on the same data. A MASE of 0.5 means the model's average error is half the size of the naive forecast's error; a MASE above 1 means the model is doing worse than just guessing the last value. This scaling is what lets you compare forecasting skill across very different series, where the raw error sizes are not comparable.

MASE = MAE / MAE_naive, where MAE_naive is the mean absolute error of a naive forecast (usually the previous value) on the same data; RMSSE = √(mean((yₜ₊ₕ − ŷₜ₊ₕ)²) / mean((yₜ − yₜ₋₁)²)) does the same with squared errors. Both are unitless: 1 means matching naive performance exactly, above 1 is worse than naive, below 1 is better. This course calls the naive baseline 'persistence,' so reporting MASE is the same idea as always reporting a model's error next to persistence's error, expressed as one ratio instead of two numbers.

Scaled metrics solve a real comparability problem MAE and RMSE alone cannot: an MAE of 3 mph at a free-flowing station and an MAE of 3 mph at a congested, low-speed station represent very different levels of skill, since 3 mph is a much bigger relative error at low speeds, but MASE and RMSSE normalize both against how hard each series actually is to forecast. This is why the M4 and M5 forecasting competitions standardized on scaled metrics for judging thousands of dissimilar series at once, and why this course adopts the same convention across stations. A subtlety: the naive baseline's own error is itself computed on some reference period, and if that period is unusually calm or volatile, the scaled metric can look artificially good or bad even though nothing about the model changed.

MASE and RMSSE differ the way MAE and RMSE differ, MASE is robust to a few large errors because it uses absolute values, RMSSE is more sensitive because it squares errors, so reporting both, as M5 effectively did, gives a fuller picture than either alone. Averaging a scaled metric across many series is itself a modeling choice: an unweighted average treats a quiet detector and a heavily trafficked mainline as equally important, while a volume-weighted average reflects real-world impact more faithfully, and the choice changes which model looks best. A common mistake is scaling by a naive-forecast error computed on the test period itself rather than a separate, prior period, which quietly leaks test-period difficulty into the very denominator meant to make the metric fair.

In production forecasting systems tracking thousands of series, MASE-style scaled metrics are what actually appear on dashboards, because raw MAE or RMSE aggregated across heterogeneous series is close to meaningless as a single number, while a properly weighted average MASE tells a team whether the fleet of models is beating the cheap baseline it would otherwise fall back to. The open engineering question is less about the formula and more about the reference: as a system's naive baseline itself improves, a fixed historical baseline stops being a fair yardstick, so mature systems periodically refresh what 'naive' means and re-baseline every reported scaled metric, a bookkeeping cost that is easy to neglect until old dashboards quietly stop meaning what they used to.

initialization.def: The rule for picking a network's very first, random weights, scaled so early activations and gradients stay neither tiny nor huge.
levels: Before a network has learned anything, it starts with random numbers for its weights, and how big those first random numbers are matters. It's like blowing up a balloon before a party: too little air and it's floppy and useless, too much and it pops before the party starts. Initialization is just picking a sensible amount of 'air' to start with.

Initialization is the rule for picking a neural network's very first weights, before any training has happened. If the starting weights are too big, the numbers flowing through the network grow huge layer after layer; if they are too small, the numbers shrink toward zero and the network can't learn anything useful. In lesson 9's numpy network, the first layer's weights start as `rng.normal(0, sqrt(2/d), ...)`, a formula called He initialization, chosen because it plays well with ReLU. Different activation functions need different starting scales, which is why there isn't just one initialization rule.

He initialization scales a layer's starting weights by √(2/d), where d is the number of inputs to that layer, and is used before a ReLU; LeCun initialization scales by √(1/d) and suits a layer feeding a sigmoid, like the network's output layer. Xavier (or Glorot) initialization, scaling by √(2/(d_in + d_out)), is the usual choice before a tanh activation. All three exist to solve the same problem: keep the variance of activations, and later the gradients flowing backward through them, roughly constant from layer to layer, instead of shrinking toward zero or blowing up over many layers. In `rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / d), (H, d))`, the `np.sqrt(2 / d)` is exactly this scale, used as the standard deviation of the random starting weights.

Initialization matters because a deep network's forward and backward passes are both repeated multiplications, and if each layer's typical weight scale pushes activations, or gradients, up or down by even a small constant factor, that factor compounds exponentially over many layers into vanishing or exploding values before any learning happens. He, Xavier and LeCun initialization are all variance-preserving schemes derived by working out, for a given activation function's typical behavior, what starting variance keeps a layer's output variance close to its input variance; He accounts for ReLU zeroing out roughly half its inputs, which is why its constant is 2/d rather than Xavier's 1/(d_in + d_out) average. Getting this wrong doesn't usually crash training outright; it more often shows up as a loss that never moves or stalls quickly, which is why lesson 9's practical rule is to check that the loss falls on a tiny subset before trusting a longer run. Modern architectures increasingly fold this concern into normalization layers rather than relying on initialization alone, but initialization still sets the state training starts from before any normalization statistics exist.

The variance-preserving derivations behind He and Xavier initialization are exact for a linear or piecewise-linear network under simplifying independence assumptions that stop holding once residual connections, normalization layers, or unusual activations are involved, which is why very deep modern architectures still need normalization and careful initialization together, not one or the other alone. A subtlety many practitioners miss is that these formulas assume a specific fan-in or fan-out convention, and scaling by the wrong dimension of a weight matrix silently produces a badly initialized network without any error being raised. Initialization also interacts with optimizer choice: Adam's per-parameter adaptive scaling makes it noticeably more forgiving of a slightly-off initialization than plain SGD is, which is part of why initialization mistakes are caught early under SGD and go unnoticed longer under Adam. For architectures with residual connections specifically, some schemes deliberately start the residual branch near zero, so the network begins close to the identity function and only gradually learns to deviate from it, a different philosophy from keeping every layer's variance constant.

At production scale, initialization is rarely tuned by hand for a new architecture; teams reuse the scheme published alongside a reference implementation and treat deviating from it as a research question in its own right, since a subtly wrong initialization can cost days of wasted training runs before anyone traces a stalled loss back to it. Very large models increasingly use initialization schemes tied explicitly to depth or width, scaling the starting variance down as the number of layers grows, because the classical per-layer formulas derived for a handful of layers understate how much compounding happens across a hundred. On-device and laptop-scale models rarely hit these extreme-depth regimes, so the classical He or Xavier formulas remain the right default there. An open question, revisited with nearly every new architecture family, is whether a better initialization can substitute for some of what normalization layers currently do, trading a one-time setup choice for ongoing per-batch computation.

lora.def: A way to fine-tune a huge pretrained model cheaply by training only a small pair of add-on matrices instead of all its weights.
levels: Imagine a huge coloring book that's already almost perfect, and instead of redrawing every page you just add a few small stickers on top to change it a little. LoRA is a way of teaching a giant, already-smart computer program a new trick by adding just a few small new pieces instead of changing the whole huge thing.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, is a trick for adjusting a huge pretrained model, like a large language model, without touching almost any of its original weights. Instead of retraining billions of numbers, LoRA adds a small pair of new matrices next to each of the model's big weight matrices and only trains those; the original weights stay frozen. Because the added matrices are tiny compared to the original, this uses far less memory and time than retraining the whole model, which matters a lot on a laptop with limited memory. The 'low-rank' part means the two small matrices are shaped so their product can only represent a limited, compressed kind of change, not just anything.

A weight matrix W in a pretrained model normally has far more numbers than are needed to represent any one small adjustment to it, so LoRA freezes W entirely and instead learns two small matrices A and B whose product ΔW = B·A is added during the forward pass: output = Wx + BAx. If W is, say, 4096 × 4096, A and B might be 4096 × 8 and 8 × 4096, thousands of times fewer trainable numbers than fine-tuning W directly. Because the frozen weights never change, LoRA also lets you swap in a different small A/B pair for a different task without storing a whole separate copy of the giant model. On a memory-limited machine like a 16 GB Mac mini, this is often the only realistic way to fine-tune a multi-billion-parameter model at all.

LoRA is one instance of a broader family of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, trading the full expressiveness of unrestricted fine-tuning for a large reduction in trainable parameters, memory and storage per task. The rank r of A and B, how few dimensions the update squeezes through, is the key hyperparameter: too small and the model can't represent the needed adjustment well; larger recovers more of full fine-tuning's flexibility at the cost of more trainable parameters, though even fairly small ranks (8 to 64) work surprisingly well in practice. Because ΔW is added at inference time, LoRA adapters can be merged back into W after training, producing a model with no extra runtime cost, or kept separate and swapped per task at some added latency. LoRA is usually applied only to specific weight matrices, most commonly attention's query and value projections, rather than every weight, itself a design choice with real accuracy tradeoffs. Compared to earlier adapter methods that insert whole extra layers into the forward path, LoRA's additive, mergeable structure is part of why it became the default parameter-efficient method.

The empirical success of very low-rank updates is itself a subtle finding: it suggests the useful adaptation to a large pretrained model's behavior lives in a much lower-dimensional space than its raw parameter count would suggest, an intrinsic-dimensionality argument with roots in earlier fine-tuning research. Which layers to apply LoRA to, and at what rank, remains largely empirical rather than theoretically settled, and the right choice can differ meaningfully between a classification task and a generation task on the same base model. LoRA composes awkwardly with quantized base models unless done carefully, which is what QLoRA addresses, backpropagating through a frozen, quantized W while still training full-precision A and B, letting a much larger base model fit the same memory budget. A practitioner mistake is assuming LoRA is a free lunch with no accuracy cost relative to full fine-tuning; on tasks needing a substantial shift in behavior rather than an adaptation at the margins, full fine-tuning or a higher rank still measurably wins.

At production scale, LoRA and its variants are the standard way to serve many customized versions of one base model cheaply: the frozen base weights are shared across customers or tasks, and only the small per-task A/B matrices need to be stored and loaded, a large win for memory and deployment cost when many fine-tuned variants exist. On-device personalization depends on this specifically: a phone or laptop can plausibly store and swap many small LoRA adapters for a shared base model, where storing many full fine-tuned copies would not fit at all. Serving infrastructure for many simultaneous LoRA adapters against one base model, batching requests that use different adapters efficiently, is itself an active systems research area. The open question that matters most in practice is less about LoRA's mechanics, now well understood, and more about which rank and which layers to adapt for a new task without expensive trial and error.

normalizing-flow.def: A generative model built from a chain of invertible transformations, turning noise into data (and back) while computing an exact likelihood.
levels: Imagine a lump of clay that a sculptor slowly reshapes, step by careful step, into a statue, and every step can also be undone to get the clay back. A normalizing flow is a computer version of that: it reshapes plain random noise, step by reversible step, into something that looks like real data, like a picture or a traffic pattern.

A normalizing flow is a generative model, one that makes new, realistic-looking data, built from a chain of small transformations that can each be run forward or backward. Starting from simple random noise, running the chain forward produces something that looks like real data; running the chain backward on a real example turns it back into noise. Because every step is exactly reversible, a normalizing flow can calculate exactly how likely any given piece of data is under the model, which a GAN cannot do at all and a VAE can only estimate. This is unusual among generative models: sharper guarantees about likelihood, at the cost of needing every transformation to be invertible by design.

A normalizing flow builds a complicated probability distribution out of a simple one, usually a standard normal, by passing samples through a sequence of invertible functions z = f_K(...f_2(f_1(x))...), each chosen so both the function and its inverse are cheap to compute and its Jacobian's determinant is cheap to track. That determinant is what lets the model report an exact likelihood: the change-of-variables formula says the transformed density is the original density divided by the absolute value of that determinant. Sampling new data means running the chain forward from simple noise; evaluating how likely a real example is means running the chain backward and multiplying in each step's determinant correction. This exactness is the flow's selling point among the generative families (GAN, VAE, flow, diffusion): a GAN gives sharp samples with no likelihood at all, a VAE gives only a bound, and a flow gives the real number.

The design problem in building a normalizing flow is finding transformations expressive enough for complex real data while keeping their Jacobian determinant tractable, since a naive transformation's determinant costs as much to compute as the transformation itself is large, defeating the purpose. Coupling layers (RealNVP, Glow) solve this by splitting the input into two halves and transforming one using a function of the other, making the Jacobian triangular and its determinant just the product of its diagonal, cheap regardless of how complex that function is. Autoregressive flows take this further, conditioning each output dimension on all previous ones, trading parallelism at sampling time for even more expressive transformations. Because every layer must be invertible, flows are architecturally more constrained than a GAN's generator or a VAE's decoder, part of why, despite their exact likelihoods, flows have not matched GANs' or diffusion's sample quality on images. Flows are also used as a component inside other models, most notably replacing a VAE's simple Gaussian posterior with something more expressive, closing some of the gap between the VAE's bound and the true likelihood.

The invertibility constraint that makes flows exact also makes them expensive relative to GANs and diffusion models at comparable sample quality, the central reason they have not displaced diffusion for high-fidelity image or audio generation, even though their exact likelihood is theoretically more principled than diffusion's variational bound. Continuous normalizing flows, defined by an ordinary differential equation rather than a finite stack of discrete layers, connect flows directly to the same machinery, score-based modeling and diffusion's SDE formulation, that diffusion uses, driving recent work unifying the two families theoretically. A subtlety often missed: a flow's exact likelihood is exact only up to the model class it can represent; a poorly-suited transformation family still fits real data badly even though the reported likelihood always exists and looks precise. For non-image data, flows are a genuinely strong choice specifically because exact likelihood evaluation, not just sampling, is often what's needed, for anomaly scoring or uncertainty estimation, unlike GANs or plain diffusion.

In production, normalizing flows show up less as a headline image generator, where diffusion dominates, and more wherever an exact, differentiable density is genuinely required: anomaly detection, density estimation for scientific or sensor data, and as a building block inside larger models needing a flexible, tractable prior or posterior. Their invertible, deterministic structure also makes flows attractive for lossless or near-lossless compression, since an exact likelihood model is directly usable as an entropy coder. On-device deployment favors flows in narrow cases where their moderate compute cost and exact density matter more than raw sample fidelity, flagging an unusual sensor reading rather than generating a picture. An open research question is whether flow-based and diffusion-based modeling will keep converging into one framework, since the mathematics underlying both, continuous-time transformations of a simple base distribution, is already substantially shared.

perplexity.def: A language model's evaluation score: roughly, how surprised the model is by held-out text, on average, per token. Lower is better.
levels: Imagine playing a guessing game where you try to guess the next word in a story before it's read aloud. Perplexity measures how surprised you'd be, on average, by each next word; a model that guesses well is rarely surprised, so it gets a low, good perplexity score.

Perplexity is the standard way to score how good a language model is at predicting text it hasn't seen before. For every word, or token, in a piece of held-out text, the model gives a probability to what the actual next word turns out to be; perplexity combines all of those probabilities into one number that says, roughly, how many equally-likely choices the model was confused between on average. A perfect model that always assigns probability 1 to the correct next word would have a perplexity of 1; a bad model that's often surprised has a much higher one. Lower perplexity means the model predicts the actual text better.

Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-probability the model assigns to each token: perplexity = exp(−(1/N) Σ log p(token_i)), where N is the number of tokens and p(token_i) is the probability given to the actual next token at each step. This is the same quantity as cross-entropy loss, just exponentiated, so a model trained by minimizing cross-entropy is, by construction, also minimizing its perplexity. A perplexity of 20 means the model was, on average, about as uncertain as if it had to guess uniformly among 20 equally likely next tokens, even though its real predictions are rarely that uniform. Perplexity is only comparable between models that share the same tokenizer and vocabulary, since a model with a bigger vocabulary starts out facing more possible next tokens to be uncertain among.

Perplexity generalizes the classical language-modeling evaluation used for n-gram models directly to neural and large language models, and remains the standard intrinsic metric for how well a model has learned a text distribution's statistics, separate from downstream task performance. Because it is computed per token and sensitive to tokenizer and vocabulary choices, perplexity numbers are not comparable across models trained with different tokenizers, a common mistake when comparing published results. A model can have excellent perplexity on its training distribution while performing poorly on instruction-following or reasoning tasks, since predicting the next token well and being a useful assistant are related but distinct objectives, which is why modern evaluation supplements perplexity with task-specific benchmarks. Perplexity is also domain-sensitive: a model's perplexity on news text and on incident-report shorthand full of route numbers and abbreviations can differ substantially at the same overall training quality, since the two domains have very different token-level predictability.

Perplexity's relationship to downstream capability is empirically strong but imperfect: models with similar perplexity can differ meaningfully in reasoning or instruction-following ability, and the field has moved toward task-specific evaluation partly because perplexity improvements plateau while real capability gains, particularly from fine-tuning and alignment, continue past that plateau. Benchmark and training-data contamination is a specific hazard for perplexity comparisons across models, since a model that has seen an evaluation text, or something very similar, during pretraining reports an artificially low perplexity on it that doesn't reflect genuine generalization. Perplexity is also awkward to compare across domains with very different token-level entropy, a highly repetitive domain naturally yields lower perplexity than an information-dense one regardless of model quality. Practitioners sometimes conflate a low training-set perplexity with a well-trained model without checking held-out perplexity, missing straightforward overfitting a validation split would catch immediately.

In production, perplexity remains a cheap, fast regression check during pretraining and continued pretraining, catching data pipeline bugs or training instabilities long before an expensive downstream evaluation would, even though it is rarely the metric that determines whether a model ships. For a fine-tuned or adapted model, a rising perplexity on a held-out domain sample is one of the simplest drift signals available, worth monitoring even when the deployed system's real success metric is something else, like extraction accuracy. The open engineering question industry-wide is how much weight to put on perplexity relative to the growing suite of task-specific and human evaluations, since perplexity is cheap and automatic but understood to be a necessary, not sufficient, signal of a model's real usefulness.
