Differential privacy protects individuals, not groups or trends, it says nothing about whether the underlying data itself is biased or wrong, and it composes worse than intuition suggests, advanced composition theorems, roughly square-root-of-k growth instead of linear k for k releases with a small delta, are needed to get useful budgets for systems that release many statistics over time, which is exactly what a continuously-monitored traffic system does. Local differential privacy, where each person randomizes their own data before it ever leaves their device, gives a stronger trust model, no central party ever sees true data, at the cost of much larger noise. Choosing epsilon in practice is a policy decision dressed as a technical parameter, there is no principled 'correct' epsilon, only a utility-privacy tradeoff a team has to justify explicitly and document.

Differential privacy is deployed at real scale in operating systems and by statistical agencies specifically because it is the one privacy technique with a provable, composable guarantee rather than a heuristic, like k-anonymity, that can fail unpredictably against a determined attacker. The research and engineering frontier is utility at practical privacy budgets under continual release, exactly the setting a streaming traffic system creates, since every new hourly release spends more of a shared, non-renewable privacy budget, and no released statistic can ever be un-released.

ndcg.def: A ranking metric that rewards putting the most relevant items near the top of a list, discounting items further down, and normalizing so a perfect ranking always scores 1.
levels: NDCG is a way of grading a top-ten list: getting the very best thing to spot number one is worth much more than getting it to spot number ten.

NDCG scores how good a ranked list is by giving more credit for relevant items near the top than for relevant items buried further down, since a real user mostly looks at the top of a list anyway. It's normalized against the best possible ordering of the same items, so a perfect ranking always scores exactly 1, no matter how many items are in the list, which makes scores comparable across different lists.

Discounted cumulative gain, DCG, sums each item's relevance divided by a discount that grows with its position, roughly relevance divided by log base 2 of (position plus 1), so an item at position 1 counts almost fully while the same item at position 10 counts much less. NDCG divides that DCG by the DCG of the best possible ordering of the same items, the 'ideal DCG,' giving a score between 0 and 1 that's comparable across lists of different lengths or with different numbers of relevant items. NDCG at k, like NDCG at 10, only scores the top k positions, which matches how a dashboard or search result is actually used, since nobody scrolls to position 500.

NDCG's log-discount is a design choice, not a law: it encodes the assumption that a user's attention decays roughly logarithmically down a ranked list, which is a reasonable approximation for many interfaces but not derived from first principles. Unlike precision or recall at k, NDCG uses graded relevance, an item can be 'somewhat' or 'very' relevant, not just relevant or not, which is why it's the standard metric when ranking quality genuinely varies in degree, several stations at real risk versus one clearly worst station, rather than being a binary judgment. Computing it requires the ideal ranking, which is easy when relevance is known for every candidate but becomes an estimation problem itself under the same exposure bias that makes offline ranking evaluation hard in general.

NDCG, like every offline ranking metric, is computed only over items that were actually shown and judged, so it inherits exposure bias exactly as raw offline evaluation does, an item that would have ranked well but was never surfaced to be judged simply never enters the calculation, which is why NDCG improvements measured offline don't always survive contact with a live system. Position-bias correction methods attempt to account for the fact that an item's observed relevance is itself a function of both true relevance and its position in whatever ranking produced the log, entangling the very thing NDCG is trying to measure with the process that generated the training data. Reporting NDCG alongside simpler metrics, precision at k, which a non-technical audience reads more easily, is common practice specifically because NDCG's log-discount, while principled, is less immediately interpretable to a stakeholder deciding whether a ranking is good enough to ship.

At production scale, NDCG and its many position-aware relatives are standard for offline ranking evaluation but are always paired with online experiments before a ranking change ships, precisely because no offline metric, however well-motivated, fully captures how real exposure and real user behavior interact with a new ranking. For a public dashboard ranking road segments by risk, the open design question isn't computing NDCG correctly, that's mechanical, but choosing what 'relevant' means in the first place: a segment that became a bottleneck, one with a near-miss, one that affects the most drivers, each a defensible and different notion of relevance the metric would score differently.

demographic-parity.def: Different mathematical definitions of a 'fair' model that generally cannot all hold at once: demographic parity means every group gets flagged at the same rate; equalized odds, or equal error rates, means every group has the same true- and false-positive rate; calibration means a score means the same real chance of the outcome in every group.
levels: There's more than one way to be fair, and they can actually disagree with each other: making sure every neighborhood gets the same number of warnings is a different kind of fair than making sure the warnings are equally right everywhere.

Demographic parity means every group gets flagged, alerted, approved, and so on, at the same rate, regardless of whether that's actually accurate for each group. Equalized odds, or equal error rates, instead means the model is wrong in the same way for every group, catching the same share of real cases and raising the same share of false alarms everywhere. These two definitions of fair usually can't both be satisfied at the same time if the groups genuinely have different underlying rates of the thing being predicted, which is a mathematical fact, not a failure of effort.

Demographic parity requires the share of each group that gets flagged to be equal, full stop, even if that means over-alerting a low-risk group or under-alerting a high-risk one to make the numbers match. Equalized odds instead requires equal true-positive and equal false-positive rates across groups: among people who really will experience the outcome, an equal share get flagged in every group, and likewise among people who won't. Calibration within groups means a score of 0.8 really does mean an 80 percent chance in every group, not just on average. Whenever groups have different true base rates for the outcome, these three cannot all hold simultaneously, a provable impossibility result, not a lack of trying harder, so choosing which one matters for a given decision is a value judgment the numbers alone can't settle.

The formal names for these are independence, demographic parity: the score is statistically independent of the group, separation, equalized odds: the score is independent of the group given the true outcome, equal error rates, and sufficiency, calibration: the outcome is independent of the group given the score. Any two of the three can generally be satisfied together only in degenerate cases, equal base rates across groups, or a perfect predictor, which is why choosing a fairness criterion for a real deployment is inescapably a decision about which kind of unfairness is more acceptable, not a technical optimization with one right answer. Mitigation techniques, reweighting the training data, adding a fairness constraint during training, or adjusting thresholds per group after training, can move a model toward one criterion, but always at some cost in overall accuracy that should be measured and reported explicitly, not assumed to be small.

Where a model's error rates differ across groups often traces back to earlier stages, measurement, the label itself is a noisier proxy for the true outcome in some groups than others, fewer detectors in some neighborhoods here, representation, fewer examples from some groups in training, or deployment, the same model used differently by different groups, which means a purely post-hoc statistical fix at the model layer cannot repair unfairness introduced upstream. The debate over which criterion should govern a given decision shows that these aren't purely technical questions; they encode different, sometimes irreconcilable, views about what fairness means for a specific decision and its consequences. Long-run dynamics complicate this further: a fair-looking decision rule today can produce unfair outcomes over time if it changes the population it's applied to, a feedback loop closely related to performative prediction.

In a deployed public system, the choice among these criteria is organizational and legal as much as technical, made through a documented process, an impact assessment, a review board, rather than by whichever engineer happens to write the threshold code, precisely because the choice is a value judgment with real consequences for real people. The research frontier includes fairness under distribution shift and feedback, a criterion satisfied at launch can drift as the model's own decisions change the population, and there is no consensus, technical or otherwise, on which criterion should govern which class of public decision.

api.def: A fixed set of requests one program is allowed to send another and the answers it will get back, so two programs can talk without either seeing the other's code.
levels: An API is like a menu at a restaurant: you don't walk into the kitchen and cook the food yourself, you just point at what you want on the menu and a waiter brings it back. A computer program does the same thing when it wants information from another program, it asks in a way the other program already understands, and waits for the answer to come back.

An API, short for application programming interface, is a fixed set of questions one computer program is allowed to ask another one, and the answers it's allowed to get back. Instead of reading through someone else's whole program to figure out how it works, you just use the API it publishes: ask for exactly this, in exactly this shape, and you'll get back exactly that. In this course, the 511 traffic service and the PeMS system both publish an API, so the collector scripts can ask them for current data instead of a person visiting a website and copying numbers by hand. An API is a promise about what a program will answer, not the program's actual code.

Most modern APIs on the web are called over HTTP: a script sends a request to a URL, sometimes with an API key attached, and the service sends back a response, usually as JSON, that the script then parses. `requests.get(url, params={'api_key': KEY})` is exactly this: it builds and sends the request, and `.json()` on the result turns the reply into a Python dictionary the rest of the script can use. An API also defines what happens when something goes wrong, an HTTP status code like 404 (not found) or 429 (too many requests), which a robust script checks rather than assuming every call succeeds. In this course, 511's and PeMS's APIs are each just a documented set of URLs and parameters, and the whole point of the collector scripts is calling them correctly and saving what comes back.

An API is a contract, not an implementation: it specifies the shape of a request and a response, but says nothing about how the service behind it actually computes that response, which is exactly what lets a service change its internals freely as long as the API's shape stays the same. A REST API, the dominant style for services like 511, maps each kind of request onto an HTTP verb (GET to read, POST to create) and a URL, and returns structured data, usually JSON, that a client parses without needing any special client library. APIs version themselves, `/v1/`, `/v2/`, precisely because breaking that contract, renaming a field, changing what a parameter means, breaks every client that already depends on the old shape, so a mature API changes additively where it can and deprecates old versions slowly rather than silently. Authentication (an API key, or a more structured token) exists so the service can identify who's calling, apply rate limits per caller, and revoke access to one caller without affecting everyone else. Calling an external API also means depending on someone else's uptime and their own rate limits, which is why a collector script has to handle a slow, wrong, or absent response as a normal case, not an exception.

An API's documentation and its actual behavior can drift apart in practice, undocumented rate limits, fields that are silently deprecated, response shapes that change without a version bump, which is why a serious integration treats the API's real, observed behavior as the ground truth and writes tests against it rather than trusting the docs alone. Idempotency is a real design property some APIs offer and others don't: an idempotent request (like a plain GET, or a well-designed POST with a client-supplied request ID) can be safely retried after a timeout without risk of double-counting, while a non-idempotent one can't, which matters directly for a collector script deciding whether to retry a failed call. Pagination, an API returning results a page at a time rather than all at once, is a common source of subtle bugs when a client stops after the first page without checking whether more pages exist, silently under-collecting data for months before anyone notices the gap. The tradeoff between polling an API on a schedule and being pushed updates via a webhook is really a tradeoff in who bears the cost of freshness: polling wastes calls on unchanged data but needs no infrastructure on the client's end, while a webhook is efficient but requires the client to run something that can receive an incoming call at any time.

At production scale, an internal API is treated as a versioned, owned contract between teams, changes go through the same review as any other interface, because a silently breaking API change can take down every downstream service that calls it at once, often the exact same failure mode as the training-serving skew problems that show up elsewhere in this course's data pipeline. Public-facing APIs at Apple's scale carry an extra dimension of cost: every field exposed becomes something millions of external clients may come to depend on, so removing or renaming a field years later is a slow, carefully staged deprecation rather than a quick edit. Internal service-to-service calls increasingly move past plain REST toward typed, schema-enforced protocols (gRPC, Protocol Buffers) precisely because they catch a mismatched field or type at build time rather than at runtime, closing the same class of silent-drift bug that a loosely-typed JSON API leaves open. An open engineering question at scale is how to keep an API's actual behavior, its rate limits, its real latency, its edge cases, honestly reflected in its documentation as both evolve, since a documentation-reality gap is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine in a demo and breaks quietly in production months later.

sine.def: Two functions that read off the horizontal and vertical position of a point walking around a circle, used whenever something repeats in a cycle, like the hours in a day.
levels: Imagine a horse on a merry-go-round. Sine tells you how far forward or back the horse is at any moment, and cosine tells you how far side to side it is, and both numbers rise and fall over and over as the merry-go-round spins around.

Picture a point walking all the way around a circle, starting at the 3 o'clock position and going counterclockwise. Cosine is that point's left-right position at any moment, and sine is its up-down position; both swing back and forth between -1 and 1 as the point goes around, and after one full trip around the circle, both start repeating exactly the same pattern. That repeating, back-and-forth shape is exactly why sine and cosine are the tools used whenever something cycles, like the hours in a day looping back to midnight.

For an angle θ measured around a circle of radius 1 (a unit circle), cos(θ) is the x-coordinate of the point at that angle and sin(θ) is its y-coordinate; θ = 0 gives cos = 1, sin = 0, and one full trip around, θ = 2π radians, brings both back to their starting values. Both functions oscillate smoothly between -1 and 1, and they're offset from each other by a quarter turn, which is exactly why using both together, rather than just one, lets you recover the original angle uniquely: sin alone can't tell 30° from 150°, since both give the same value, but the pair sin and cos together can. In Python, `math.sin(theta)` and `math.cos(theta)` (or `np.sin`, `np.cos` for a whole array of angles at once) take an angle in radians, not degrees, so a value in degrees needs to be multiplied by π/180 first. This course uses exactly this pair, `sin(2π · hour/24)` and `cos(2π · hour/24)`, to turn the hour of day into two smoothly cycling numbers instead of a raw hour value that wrongly treats 23:00 and 00:00 as far apart.

Sine and cosine are defined more generally via the unit circle rather than only via a right triangle's ratios, which is what lets them extend cleanly to any angle, including ones past 90°, and to the continuous, periodic functions used throughout signal processing and feature engineering rather than just static geometry. Their defining algebraic relationship, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem applied to a point at distance 1 from the origin, and it's the reason a sin-cos pair always lands exactly on the unit circle no matter what angle goes in. Representing a cyclic feature as a (sin, cos) pair rather than a raw angle or hour number is a specific, deliberate choice: it gives a model two smoothly varying, bounded inputs whose Euclidean distance from each other genuinely reflects how close two times of day actually are, which a raw hour number, or even a one-hot encoding of hour, does not provide on its own. Beyond time features, sine and cosine underlie Fourier analysis broadly, decomposing any periodic signal into a sum of sine and cosine waves of different frequencies, which is the same core idea scaled up from encoding one cyclic feature to modeling an entire repeating signal.

Sine and cosine are each other's derivatives up to a sign, d/dx sin(x) = cos(x) and d/dx cos(x) = -sin(x), a closed loop under differentiation that makes them uniquely convenient building blocks for anything requiring smooth, infinitely differentiable periodic behavior, exactly the property that makes a sin-cos time encoding play nicely with gradient-based models rather than introducing a discontinuity a raw modulo-24 hour value would. Choosing a single period, 24 hours, 7 days, 365 days, for a sin-cos encoding is itself an assumption that the underlying phenomenon is smoothly, evenly periodic at exactly that period, which holds reasonably well for daily traffic rhythms but poorly for something like day-of-week, where weekday and weekend behavior differ sharply rather than blending smoothly around the circle. Multiple harmonics, adding sin and cos at 2× or 3× the base frequency alongside the base pair, let a cyclic encoding capture a repeating shape that isn't a simple smooth wave, like a sharp morning commute spike, at the cost of more input features and more risk of overfitting with limited data. Numerically, sin and cos are transcendental functions computed via series approximations or lookup tables inside a math library, not exact closed-form arithmetic, so extremely large angle inputs, many full rotations before the value that actually matters, can lose precision, part of why an angle is normally reduced to one period's range before these functions are applied in a numerically careful pipeline.

At production scale, sin-cos time encodings remain a cheap, reliable default for cyclic features across many forecasting systems specifically because they're smooth, bounded, and require no learned parameters, unlike a learned embedding of time-of-day, which needs enough data per time bucket to train well and can behave unpredictably on a time never seen during training. Positional encodings in transformer architectures generalize this exact idea, using sine and cosine at many different frequencies simultaneously to give a model a smooth, unique signature for each position in a sequence, which is a direct descendant of the same trick used here for encoding hour of day, just applied to sequence position instead of time. An open research question in forecasting specifically is when a hand-built sin-cos encoding still beats a fully learned time representation, and the empirical answer generally favors the hand-built version when training data per cycle is limited and favors a learned one once there's enough data to learn subtler, non-sinusoidal periodic shapes directly.
